Charging in without knowing the rules is like turning on a machine without reading the manual — you're not brave, you're just paying tuition with your principal.

qa.q: 股市給「有能耐、能自我控制者」以小錢賺大錢的機會——你覺得自己屬於哪一種？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 股市給無經濟基礎者以小錢賺大錢的機會，對有能耐、能自我控制者是天堂；但也是「有經驗者獲金錢、有金錢者獲經驗」的殘酷之地，血淋淋的慘痛教訓常有發生。你以為自己屬於「有能耐」那一類——可你的上一次交易，是「自我控制」，還是「衝動下單」？
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 The stock market gives people without capital a chance to make big money with small money; for those who are capable and can control themselves, it's heaven. But it's also a ruthless place where "the experienced get money, and the wealthy get experience" — bloody lessons are common. You think you're one of the "capable" ones — but your last trade, was it "self-control" or "impulse order"?

qa.q: 討厭風險、急著發財、自以為是、趕潮跟風、因循守舊——這串人性弱點裡，你佔幾條？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 主要是人性弱點所致：討厭風險、急著發財、自以為是、不思進取、趕潮跟風、因循守舊、斤斤計較等缺點，使大多數股民難以避開股市陷阱。你看著這串清單，心裡在想「我沒那麼嚴重」——而「沒那麼嚴重」，正是它最危險的樣子。你怕承認，自己說「沒那麼嚴重」時在逃避。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 It's mainly due to human weaknesses: aversion to risk, eagerness to get rich, self-righteousness, lack of drive, following trends, sticking to old ways, being penny-wise — these flaws make it hard for most investors to avoid the traps. As you look at this list, you're thinking, "I'm not that bad" — and "not that bad" is exactly when it's most dangerous. You're afraid to admit that when you say "not that bad," you're avoiding the truth.

qa.q: 貪小便宜、盯蠅頭小利、一點虧都不能喫、一夜暴富——你中了幾槍？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 好貪小便宜，眼睛總盯在蠅頭小利上；一點虧都不能喫，抱一夜暴發的心態，這種心態使大部分股民幾乎必然地成為輸家。這四槍你中得越多，離「必然輸家」越近——因為每一槍，都在讓你用大格局換小便宜。
qa.a_en: Hi~ 😊 Love being penny-wise but always eyeing the small stuff; can't bear to take a loss, with a get-rich-overnight mindset — this kind of attitude almost inevitably turns most stock players into losers. The more of these four bullets you catch, the closer you get to being an "inevitable loser" — because each one makes you trade your big picture for a tiny bargain.

qa.q: 兒子靠「吹蠟燭、推傭人、丟石頭」脫險——你危急時，有「脫險的招式」嗎？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 兒子被困儲存間時吹熄蠟燭、推開傭人逃跑，又丟石入塘引開追兵，靠機智脫險；小偷據此判定他已學會偷——即危急時刻懂得自保逃生。逃生不是天生的，是預演的——你從沒預演過「大跌時我怎麼辦」，危機來了當然只會慌。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 When the son was trapped in the storage room, he blew out the candle, shoved the maid aside and ran, then threw rocks into the pond to distract the pursuers—he used his wits to escape. The thief concluded from this that the boy had already learned to steal—meaning he knew how to save himself in a crisis. Escaping isn't something you're born with; it's something you rehearse. If you've never rehearsed 'what do I do when the market crashes,' of course you'll only panic when it actually hits.

qa.q: 先搞清規則、再定策略——你的策略，是順著市場走的，還是跟市場對著幹的？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 作者主張參與前先搞清遊戲規則，然後再製定與市場走勢相一致的應對策略；不研究規則、不順應走勢就貿然入市，等於自陷險境。你的策略如果總在「跟市場講道理」，那不是在應對市場，是在對抗市場——而對抗者的結局，故事裡寫得很清楚。你怕承認，自己總在跟市場講道理。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 The author's point is that before you participate, you need to understand the rules of the game first, then craft a strategy that aligns with how the market actually moves. If you dive in without studying the rules or going with the flow, you're basically walking into a trap. If your strategy keeps trying to 'reason with the market,' you're not responding to it—you're fighting it. And the story tells you exactly how that ends for people who fight it. You're afraid to admit that you're always trying to reason with the market.

qa.q: 想靠股市「以此為生」——你準備好長期對抗自己的弱點了嗎？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 偶然在股市賺點錢不難，但頻頻得手並不容易，要以此為生更是對自我和人性的挑戰，因為必須長期克服人性的弱點。以此為生，意味著你每天都要和「討厭風險、急著發財」的自己作戰——你以為難在技術，其實難在每天重複的自我對抗。你怕承認，自己每天要對抗的是手癢。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 Making a bit of money in the stock market by luck now and then isn't hard, but doing it consistently isn't easy. Doing it for a living is an even bigger challenge to yourself and your humanity, because you have to overcome your own weaknesses day after day. Doing this for a living means every single day you're fighting against the part of you that hates risk and wants to get rich fast. You think the hard part is the technique—but the real challenge is that daily battle with yourself. You're afraid to admit that what you're really fighting every day is your own itchy trigger finger.

qa.q: 重大事件來臨時，你是「經歷過」還是「把握住」？——這兩個詞，差在哪裡？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 重大事件往往是難得的機遇，要求投資人具備很大勇氣與敏銳的市場嗅覺；很多人即便經歷了也沒收穫，正因缺乏勇氣與對機遇的敏銳嗅覺。經歷是時間的巧合，把握是能力的結果——你上一次重大事件，是剛好碰上，還是主動抓住？你怕承認，自己只是剛好碰上。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 Major events are often rare opportunities—they demand a lot of courage and a sharp sense of market timing from investors. Many people go through them and still gain nothing, precisely because they lack that courage and that sharp nose for opportunity. Experiencing something is just a coincidence of timing; seizing it is a result of your ability. The last major event—did you just happen to be there, or did you actively grab it? You're afraid to admit that you were just there by accident.

qa.q: 入世對各行各業「既是機遇也是挑戰」——同一件事，你習慣先看到機遇，還是先看到挑戰？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 2001年12月11日中國正式加入世界貿易組織；對各行各業既是機遇也是挑戰，原本不能走出國門的商品可以走出去了，這是機遇，受保護行業失去保護則是挑戰。機遇和挑戰是同一枚硬幣的兩面——你總先看到挑戰，不是因為挑戰多，是因為挑戰讓你安心（可以不動），機遇讓你害怕（必須行動）。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 On December 11, 2001, China officially joined the WTO. It was both an opportunity and a challenge for every industry: products that couldn't go abroad before could now go out—that's the opportunity. And protected industries losing that protection—that's the challenge. Opportunity and challenge are two sides of the same coin. You always see the challenge first, not because there's more challenge, but because challenge feels safe (you don't have to move), while opportunity scares you (because you have to act).

qa.q: 知識產權、資本市場開放——談判桌上爭得最兇的，往往是最值錢的信息。你關心過這類「政策級」信息嗎？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 一個是知識產權的保護，另一個是資本市場的對外開放；這是爭論的焦點問題，這些問題不解決就有可能影響中國加入WTO。爭執越激烈的地方，越藏著未來的方向——你只盯著個股的消息，等於在大海裡只看浪花，不看洋流。你怕承認，自己只盯浪花不看洋流。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 One is intellectual property protection, the other is opening up the capital market—these were the focal points of debate. If these issues weren't resolved, they could delay China's entry into the WTO. The fiercer the argument, the more it hides the direction of the future. If you only stare at individual stock news, it's like staring at the waves in the ocean while ignoring the currents. You're afraid to admit that all you watch are the waves, not the currents.

qa.q: 「資本市場開放和股市息息相關」——你覺得這句話跟你帳戶裡的錢有關係嗎？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 要加入WTO就必須徹底解決資本市場開放等問題；資本市場開放和股市息息相關，作為股票市場的投資人，不能不重視這些信息。制度一變，所有股票的定價邏輯都要重寫——你覺得「跟我的錢無關」，是因為你還沒學會從制度看股價。你怕承認，自己覺得制度與錢無關。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 To join the WTO, issues like capital market opening had to be fully resolved. The capital market opening is directly tied to the stock market, so as a stock market investor, you can't afford to ignore this kind of information. When the system changes, the pricing logic of every single stock gets rewritten. When you think 'this has nothing to do with my money,' it's because you haven't learned to read stock prices through the lens of the system. You're afraid to admit that you believe systems and money have nothing to do with each other.

qa.q: 「很多人經歷了也沒收穫」——你上一次重大事件，收穫了什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 原因是缺乏足夠的勇氣以及對機遇的敏銳嗅覺；重大事件可遇不可求，唯有勇氣加嗅覺，才能把事件轉化為實實在在的收穫。勇氣讓你敢動，嗅覺讓你知道往哪動——你兩樣都缺，於是隻能做「事後諸葛亮」，在別人的收穫裡驗證自己的判斷。你怕承認，自己只會事後諸葛亮。
keywords: 很多人經歷了也沒收穫
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 The reason is a lack of courage and a lack of sharp instinct for opportunity. Major events are rare—you can't count on them. Only with courage plus instinct can you turn an event into real gains. Courage lets you make a move; instinct tells you which way to move. You're missing both, so all you can do is play Monday-morning quarterback, validating your own judgment through other people's wins. You're afraid to admit that you're only ever wise after the fact.

qa.q: 上證1500點、信心最受打擊——那個「最沒人敢買」的時候，你敢買嗎？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 中國股市低迷不振，上證指數一直徘徊在1500點左右，投資人對市場未來發展大都持懷疑態度，經過2001年以來的下跌，人們的信心遭受到最嚴重的打擊。信心最受打擊的時候，往往是機會最豐厚的時候——可你敢不敢在那時買入，決定了你是「收穫者」還是「見證者」。你怕承認，自己不敢在打擊最深時買。
qa.a_en: Hey there! 😊 China's stock market has been sluggish, with the Shanghai Composite Index hovering around 1,500 points. Most investors are skeptical about the market's future. After the decline since 2001, people's confidence has taken its hardest hit. The moment confidence hits rock bottom is often when opportunities are richest—but whether you dare to buy at that moment determines if you're a 'harvester' or a 'bystander.' You're afraid to admit that you don't dare to buy when the blow is deepest.

qa.q: 作者「摘抄公開文獻」來研究歷史機遇——你研究機會時，會去翻原始文獻嗎？還是隻看二手解讀？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 作者主張仔細研究中國加入WTO後有關資本市場開放的承諾，摘抄相關公開文獻，帶領讀者一起回顧這段歷史機遇。一手文獻是事實，二手解讀是觀點——你只看二手解讀，等於喫別人嚼過的東西，營養和風險都由別人定。你怕承認，自己只喫二手解讀。
qa.a_en: Hey there! 😊 The author advocates carefully studying China's commitments to opening up its capital markets after joining the WTO, excerpting relevant public documents, and leading readers through this historical opportunity together. Primary sources are facts; secondary interpretations are opinions—if you only look at secondary interpretations, it's like eating what others have already chewed, with the nutrition and risks determined by others. You're afraid to admit that you only consume secondary interpretations.

qa.q: 把握重大事件需要「勇氣＋嗅覺」——你誠實地問自己：你缺的是哪一個？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 需要很大勇氣以及敏銳的市場嗅覺，兩者缺一不可；具備者才能把可遇不可求的重大事件變成難得的投資機遇。缺勇氣的人，看得到不敢動；缺嗅覺的人，敢動但看不懂——你先承認自己缺哪個，纔有機會補哪個。
qa.a_en: Hey there! 😊 It takes a lot of courage as well as sharp market instincts—both are indispensable. Only those who have both can turn rare, once-in-a-lifetime major events into valuable investment opportunities. Those lacking courage see it but don't dare to act; those lacking instincts dare to act but don't understand—admit which one you're missing first, and only then can you have a chance to fill that gap.

qa.q: 「緩衝期5年，2006年迎來全新時代」——一個5年後的判斷，你願意提前佈局嗎？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 主張資本市場全面對外開放的緩衝期是5年，2006年中國資本市場將迎來一個全新的時代；銀行須擴大規模以提升競爭力，這對已上市銀行是長期重大利好。5年太長，長到多數人沒耐心；可正是因為沒耐心，提前佈局的人才賺得到錢——你等的不是5年，是「馬上見效」。你怕承認，自己要的從來是馬上見效。
qa.a_en: Hey there! 😊 The author argues that the buffer period for fully opening the capital market is five years, and that in 2006, China's capital market will usher in a brand-new era. Banks must expand their scale to enhance competitiveness, which is a major long-term positive for listed banks. Five years is too long—too long for most people's patience. But precisely because of that impatience, those who position themselves early are the ones who make money—what you're waiting for isn't five years; it's 'immediate results.' You're afraid to admit that what you've always wanted is immediate results.

qa.q: 外幣業務即時放開、人民幣業務5年逐步開放——這些「時間表」，你看懂了什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 即時取消外資銀行外匯業務的客戶對象限制並擴充業務範圍；人民幣業務按5年時間表分五批開放地域，加入後2年內向中資企業、5年內向所有中國客戶開放，5年後享受國民待遇。時間表不是新聞，是地圖——它標出了資金將流向哪裡；你看不懂地圖，就只能等別人走完了跟著走。你怕承認，自己總等別人走完纔跟。
qa.a_en: Hey there! 😊 The immediate lifting of restrictions on foreign banks' foreign-currency business clients and expanding their business scope; RMB business opens up geographically in five batches over a five-year timeline, opening to Chinese enterprises within two years and to all Chinese customers within five years, with national treatment after five years. The timeline isn't news—it's a map. It marks where capital will flow. If you can't read the map, you'll just wait for others to finish and follow behind. You're afraid to admit that you always wait until others finish before following.

qa.q: B股直通、特別會員、合資基金、合資券商——四項開放，你從中看到了「誰會來買」嗎？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 外國證券機構可不經中方中介直接從事B股交易；駐華代表處可成為證券交易所特別會員；可設中外合資基金管理公司，外資比例加入時不超33%、3年內不超49%；3年內可設合資證券公司，外資比例不超過三分之一。開放的四項內容，句句都在說「外資要來了」——外資來了買什麼？這纔是你該想的問題。你怕承認自己從沒想過。
qa.a_en: Hey there! 😊 Foreign securities institutions may directly engage in B-share trading without Chinese intermediaries; representative offices in China may become special members of stock exchanges; Sino-foreign joint venture fund management companies may be established, with foreign equity not exceeding 33% upon accession and not exceeding 49% within three years; joint venture securities companies may be established within three years, with foreign equity not exceeding one-third. Every one of these four opening measures is saying, 'Foreign capital is coming.' What will foreign capital buy when it arrives? That's the question you should be thinking about. You're afraid to admit you've never thought about it.

qa.q: 企業形式、開放地域、業務範圍——開放分三路推進，你看到了哪一路的機會？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 分企業形式、開放地域、業務範圍三方面：非壽險加入時合資外資可達51%，2年內可設獨資；壽險合資外資不超50%；地域上3年內取消限制，業務上逐步放開健康險、團體險和養老金/年金險。三路開放是三條資金通道——你看不到通道，就只能在別人湧入時擠在門口。你怕承認，自己總在門口擠。
keywords: 你看到了哪一路的機會
qa.a_en: Hey there! 😊 It breaks down into three aspects: corporate form, geographic scope, and business scope. For non-life insurance, foreign equity in joint ventures can reach 51% upon accession, and wholly foreign-owned entities within two years; for life insurance, foreign equity in joint ventures cannot exceed 50%; geographically, restrictions are lifted within three years; business-wise, health insurance, group insurance, and pension/annuity insurance are gradually opened up. Three routes of opening are three capital channels—if you can't see the channels, you'll only be squeezing at the door when others flood in. You're afraid to admit that you're always squeezing at the door.

qa.q: 作者在「12元、沒人看好」時分批買入招行——換成你，你敢嗎？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 基於銀行必須擴大規模才能與國外資本抗衡的判斷，於2002年到2003年間分批買入招商銀行，價格分別在12元左右，視其為受惠於開放承諾、長期影響深遠的利好標的。12元買入時，市場一片蕭條——你的判斷，能不能在「別人都說不行」的時候還站得住？你怕承認，自己在別人都說不行時站不住。
qa.a_en: Hey there! 😊 Based on the judgment that banks must expand their scale to compete with foreign capital, I bought China Merchants Bank in batches between 2002 and 2003, at around 12 yuan per share, viewing it as a beneficiary of opening commitments and a longer-term positive play. When you bought at 12 yuan, the market was in a slump—can your judgment still hold when 'everyone says it's no good'? You're afraid to admit that you can't hold when everyone says it's no good.

qa.q: 買入後兩年不漲、甚至跌到6元——你熬得住「買對卻不漲」的兩年嗎？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 從復權結果看整整2年一直在11元附近震盪，期間歷經除權，2005年股價降到9元再除權至6元上下，最低見5.8元多，整個中國股市一片蕭條。買對方向卻要熬兩年，是最考驗人的部分——多數人不是看錯，是熬不住；你一熬不住，就把「對的判斷」賣在了「最蕭條的價」。你怕承認，自己就是那個熬不住的人。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 Looking at the adjusted results, the stock hovered around 11 yuan for a full two years, going through ex-rights adjustments along the way. In 2005, the price dropped to 9 yuan, then ex-rights to around 6 yuan, with a low of just over 5.8 yuan—the whole Chinese stock market was in a slump. Getting the direction right but having to endure two years of waiting—that's the real test. Most people don't get it wrong; they just can't hold on. The moment you give up, you sell your "right call" at the "most depressed price." You're afraid to admit that you're the one who couldn't hold on.

qa.q: 一片迷茫時，QFII在買、散戶在賣——同樣的市場，為什麼兩邊看到的不一樣？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 QFII大舉進入中國市場，紛紛介入中國的金融、有色金屬、資源類股票；2006年後半年藍籌股猛烈上漲，指數從1000點漲到5000點以上，QFII成為大牛市最大受益者。QFII按時間表買，散戶按心情賣——你們看的是同一張K線，用的是完全不同的尺子。你怕承認，自己的尺子量的是心情。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 QFII poured into the Chinese market, grabbing stakes in financials, non-ferrous metals, and resource stocks. In the second half of 2006, blue chips surged, and the index jumped from 1,000 points to over 5,000—QFII was the biggest winner of the bull market. QFII buys on a schedule, retail investors sell on their moods—you're all looking at the same candlestick chart, but using completely different rulers. You're afraid to admit that your ruler measures moods.

qa.q: 有人5.98元賣出招行，據說還是「當天高價」——你會不會也在「最絕望的當天」賣出？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 最為悲哀的是有人以5.98元（據說是當天高價）賣出；作者認為若能以8元買進漲到40多元，熬6年也沒人說不好，問題是過去的一切都不會再來。5.98元的賣出，不是那個人的錯，是「絕望的那一天」替所有人做的決定——你上一次在絕望中賣出，賣在了哪裡？你怕承認，自己也曾在絕望中賣出。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 The saddest part is someone selling at 5.98 yuan (supposedly the high that day). The author thinks if you could buy at 8 yuan and watch it climb to over 40 yuan, nobody would complain about enduring six years—but the problem is the past never comes back. Selling at 5.98 yuan wasn't that person's fault; it was "that day of despair" making the decision for everyone. The last time you sold in despair, where did you sell? You're afraid to admit that you, too, have sold in despair.

qa.q: 「缺少有遠見的機構」——你批評市場沒遠見時，你自己有遠見嗎？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 缺少具有遠見卓識的實力機構的支撐，這是根本原因；加入WTO的開放承諾引來世紀豪門盛宴，款待了來自海外的QFII，而國內券商即使在2006年餘痛未消也不敢大舉拓展業務。你批評機構短視，可你自己在蕭條期敢買嗎？遠見不是「事後看得懂」，是「當下敢下注」。你怕承認，自己的遠見總在事後。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 The root cause was the lack of visionary, strong institutions for support. Joining the WTO opened the door to a century-defining feast, hosting overseas QFII, while domestic brokerages, still smarting from 2006, dared not expand aggressively. You criticize institutions for being shortsighted, but would you dare to buy during a downturn? Vision isn't "understanding it in hindsight"; it's "daring to bet in the moment." You're afraid to admit your vision always comes after the fact.

qa.q: 股改對價造成「20元變6元」的落差——這種「制度性落差」，你看到的是機會還是風險？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 把握股改對價造成的股價落差，在股改推進階段逢低買入具上漲潛力、風險較低的股票，耐心持有等待填權行情兌現暴利。制度性落差是市場送來的機會——你看到的是「縮水」的恐懼，還是「空間」的興奮，決定了你是參與者還是旁觀者。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 Seize the price gap created by share reform compensation—during the reform rollout, buy stocks with upside potential and low risk at bargain prices, hold patiently, and wait for the rights-filling rally to deliver big profits. The institutional gap is a gift from the market—whether you see "shrinking" fear or "room" excitement decides if you're a player or a bystander.

qa.q: 世紀「盛宴」——你參加過幾次？還是每次都在場外聽別人講？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 因為股改影響了中國股市的思維習慣，其推進使資本市場迎來獲取巨大利益的機會，參與者能分到一杯羹，故稱世紀「盛宴」。盛宴的門票不是錢，是提前的認知——你總在開席後才聽說，不是因為運氣差，是因為你從不提前研究「下一場盛宴在哪裡」。你怕承認，自己從不提前研究下一場盛宴。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 Because share reform reshaped how the Chinese stock market thinks, its progress gave the capital market a shot at massive gains, and participants got a slice of the pie—hence the century "feast." The ticket to the feast isn't money; it's knowing ahead of time. You always hear about it after the party starts—not because you're unlucky, but because you never research "where the next feast is" in advance. You're afraid to admit you never research the next feast in advance.

qa.q: 20元變6元、一年漲3倍——聽到這種數字，你的第一念頭是「機會」還是「騙局」？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 某股票股改前每股20元左右，股改對價後不足6元，價格大幅縮水，形成巨大的利潤空間。巨大的落差，既可能是機會也可能是陷阱——區分兩者靠的不是膽子，是對「對價機制」的理解；你不理解機制，就只能用「騙局」兩個字安慰自己錯過的機會。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 One stock was around 20 yuan per share before the share reform, and after the compensation it was under 6 yuan—the price shrank dramatically, creating a huge profit space. A massive gap can be either an opportunity or a trap—what separates the two isn't guts, but understanding the "compensation mechanism." If you don't understand the mechanics, you'll just console yourself with the word "scam" for the opportunities you missed.

qa.q: 作者「4.28元買入華夏銀行」——他買的是價格，還是買的是「對事件的理解」？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 2006年9月份，作者以每股4.28元的價格買入華夏銀行股，此舉遵循了他以往穩健篩選、低價介入的投資風格。4.28元不是隨手一買，是研究之後的落點——你只看到「他買了」，看不到他之前研究了多少；看不到研究的人，會以為賺錢全靠運氣。你怕承認，自己以為賺錢全靠運氣。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 In September 2006, the author bought Huaxia Bank shares at 4.28 yuan per share, sticking to his usual style of steady screening and low-price entry. 4.28 yuan wasn't a random buy; it was a landing point after research. You only see "he bought"—you don't see how much he studied before that. People who don't see the research assume it's all luck. You're afraid to admit that you think making money is all luck.

qa.q: 20只股票、兼顧「上漲潛力＋風險較低」——你的選股，有這樣的標準嗎？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 共篩選出20只具有上漲潛力且風險較低的股票，標準兼顧上漲空間與安全性，到2007年3月左右這些股票均有3倍以上漲幅。標準是篩子，不是裝飾——你沒有標準，就只能用「感覺」篩，而感覺篩出來的，往往是別人想賣給你的。你怕承認，自己篩股票用的是感覺。
qa.a_en: Hey there～😊 In total, 20 stocks with upside potential and lower risk were screened out. The criteria balance both upside room and safety—by around March 2007, these stocks had all gained more than 3x. Criteria are a filter, not decoration—if you don't have criteria, you can only screen by "feel," and what feel screens out is often what others want to sell you. You're afraid to admit that you screen stocks by feel.

qa.q: 5.5元一口氣漲到20元、一年漲3倍——這種行情裡，你拿得住嗎？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 從2005年10月份的5.5元價格一口氣漲到20元左右的填權行情，時間約為2006年10月份前後，一年時間漲幅超過3倍。一年3倍的行情，多數人只喫到其中一段——不是行情不給機會，是你在翻倍時就急著「落袋為安」，把3倍的行情做成了1倍。你怕承認，自己總在翻倍時急著落袋。
qa.a_en: Hey there～😊 From the October 2005 price of 5.5 yuan straight up to around 20 yuan in a fill-the-gap move—that happened around October 2006, a 3x+ gain in one year. A 3x move in a year—most people only catch a piece of it. It's not that the market doesn't give chances—it's that you rush to "lock in profits" when it doubles, turning a 3x move into a 1x one. You're afraid to admit you always rush to take profits when it doubles.

qa.q: 3倍、5倍——「持股耐心」的價值，你親身體驗過嗎？還是隻在書裡讀過？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 到2007年3月份左右，20只股票都有3倍以上的漲幅；10月份左右，很多股票的漲幅都高於5倍，驗證了持股耐心的價值。耐心不是「不動」，是「拿得住確定的邏輯」——你拿不住，是因為你買的時候就沒有邏輯，只有衝動；沒有邏輯的人，當然沒有耐心。
qa.a_en: Hey there～�� By around March 2007, all 20 stocks had gained 3x+; by around October, many were up over 5x—proving the value of holding patiently. Patience isn't "doing nothing," it's "holding tight to a logic you're sure of"—you can't hold, because when you bought, you had no logic, only impulse. People without logic naturally have no patience.

qa.q: 及早識別信號、篩選低風險高潛力標的、穩健佈局、耐心持有——這四步，你卡在哪一步？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 重大制度事件會改變市場思維並帶來暴利機會，應及早識別信號、篩選低風險高潛力標的，以穩健風格佈局並耐心持有。四步環環相扣，卡住任何一步，後面全是空談——你先承認自己卡在哪，才知道該補哪裡。
keywords: 篩選低風險高潛力標的
qa.a_en: Hey there～😊 Major institutional events can shift market thinking and bring explosive profit opportunities. You should identify the signals early, screen for low-risk, high-potential targets, position with a steady style, and hold patiently. These four steps are interlocked—if any one gets stuck, everything after is empty talk. First admit where you're stuck, then you'll know what to patch.

qa.q: 「化繁為簡，安全賺錢」——你的投資，做到了哪一半？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 主張「化繁為簡，安全賺錢」：銀行業是資本市場的核心，選銀行業就是化繁為簡；維護銀行業安全有比你更重要的人和機構參與，這就是安全賺錢。化繁為簡考驗認知，安全賺錢考驗紀律——你多半兩樣都缺一點，缺認知就抓不住主線，缺紀律就守不住本金。你怕承認，自己兩樣都缺。
qa.a_en: Hey there～😊 I advocate "simplify the complex, make money safely": banking is the core of the capital market, so choosing banking is simplifying the complex; protecting banking safety involves people and institutions more important than you—that's making money safely. Simplifying tests your understanding, safe money tests your discipline—you're probably a bit short on both. Without understanding, you can't grasp the main thread; without discipline, you can't protect your capital. You're afraid to admit you're short on both.

qa.q: 銀行改制上市、藍籌回歸、股指期貨、價格低估——這麼多理由，你買股票時能列出一半嗎？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 國有銀行股份制改革陸續完成並上市，海外上市銀行及藍籌股回歸，股指期貨到來使藍籌股受大資金關照，加上銀行股相對高價股價格嚴重被低估，故看好。看好一支股票，要能列出一串理由而不是一個衝動——你列不出來，不是因為沒理由，是因為你從沒認真想過。
qa.a_en: Hey there～😊 State-owned banks completed their shareholding reforms and listed one after another, overseas-listed banks and blue chips returned, stock index futures meant big money started paying attention to blue chips, and bank stocks were severely undervalued compared to higher-priced stocks—so the outlook is bullish. To be bullish on a stock, you need to list a string of reasons, not one impulse—you can't list them, not because there are no reasons, but because you've never seriously thought it through.

qa.q: 「農行上市、股指期貨啟動之時」——你相信「啟動有標誌」嗎？還是總想搶在標誌之前？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 農行改制成功順利上市、股指期貨正式進入市場開始啟動之時，就是中國銀行股全面啟動的日子。啟動有標誌，意味著機會有跡可循——你總想搶在標誌前，是因為你怕「晚了」；可搶跑的人，往往在標誌出現前就耗盡了子彈。
keywords: 還是總想搶在標誌之前
qa.a_en: Hey there～😊 When ABC's restructuring is successfully done and it lists, and stock index futures officially enter the market and start running—that's the day China's bank stocks fully take off. A takeoff has its signs, meaning opportunity leaves a trail—you always want to jump in before the signs because you're afraid it'll be "too late." But people who jump early often burn through their bullets before the signs even appear.

qa.q: 存銀行你是客戶，買銀行股你是東家——你願意從「客戶」升級成「東家」嗎？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 存銀行你是客戶，直接買銀行股你就是東家；資本增值需靠智慧達成、需金融精英打理。面對物價上漲，負利息下直接買銀行股比存銀行更直接。當客戶省心但喫虧，當東家費心但增值——你選哪個，暴露的是你對「費心」的態度。你怕承認，自己怕費心。
qa.a_en: Hey there～😊 When you deposit money in the bank, you're a customer; when you buy bank stocks directly, you're the owner. Capital growth needs wisdom and elite financial managers to handle it. With rising prices and negative real interest, buying bank stocks directly beats depositing in the bank. Being a customer saves you worry but costs you; being the owner costs you effort but grows your wealth—which one you pick reveals your attitude toward "effort." You're afraid to admit you're afraid of the effort.

qa.q: 民生、招行、華夏、建行、工行、中行、交行——你對銀行股的瞭解，到「名字」為止嗎？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 小盤的民生銀行、招商銀行、華夏銀行，大盤的建設銀行、工商銀行、中國銀行、交通銀行等，都被視為潛力無比的優質股票。名字人人會念，區別沒幾個人知道——你能說出小盤和大盤銀行股在「彈性」上的差別嗎？說不出，就別說自己瞭解銀行股。你怕承認，自己只會念名字。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 Small-cap bank stocks like Minsheng Bank, China Merchants Bank, and Huaxia Bank, and large-cap ones like China Construction Bank, ICBC, Bank of China, and Bank of Communications are all seen as high-potential quality stocks. Anyone can say the names, but hardly anyone knows the difference—can you tell me how small-cap and large-cap bank stocks differ in "volatility"? If you can't, then don't say you know bank stocks. You're afraid to admit you can only recite names.

qa.q: 「幾十上百元的股票比比皆是，銀行股卻嚴重低估」——你敢在「被低估」時買入嗎？還是總覺得「低估有低估的理由」？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 市場上動不動就幾十甚至上百元的股票比比皆是，相比之下銀行股目前價格嚴重低估，這是對資本市場充分了解後的理性觀點，而非過激言辭。「低估有理由」這句話，常常是散戶為自己不敢行動找的藉口——判斷低估需要研究，而你用「有理由」代替了研究。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 Stocks priced at tens or even hundreds of yuan are everywhere in the market, and bank stocks are severely undervalued by comparison—this is a rational view backed by a solid understanding of the capital market, not an over-the-top statement. "There's a reason they're undervalued" is often just an excuse retail investors use to avoid taking action—judging undervaluation requires research, and you replaced research with "there's a reason."

qa.q: 「不是預測，不是總結，是加深理念」——你讀書，是為了學理念，還是為了找「明天買什麼」？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 不是對未來作預測，也不是對歷史作總結，而是希望再次加深「化繁為簡，安全賺錢」的投資理念，強調其作為全書指導原則的地位。你讀書只想找「明天買什麼」的答案，於是讀完一本書，理念沒留下，代碼記了一堆——而沒有理念的代碼，只是別人的運氣。你怕承認，自己只想找明天買什麼。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 It's not about predicting the future or summarizing history, but about reinforcing the investment philosophy of "simplify, make money safely" and highlighting its role as the guiding principle of the whole book. You read only to find "what to buy tomorrow," so after finishing a book, the philosophy doesn't stick, but you've memorized a bunch of ticker codes—and codes without a philosophy are just someone else's luck. You're afraid to admit you only want to find what to buy tomorrow.

qa.q: 「不要把後記當作買入理由」——你會不會把任何「別人看好」當作你的買入理由？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 無論如何不要把後記作為買入銀行股票的理由，一定要嚴格按書中方法充分研究，制定完整投資交易策略並嚴格執行買賣，這纔是最正確的做法。作者的告誡是：觀點可以聽，理由必須自己建——你拿「作者看好」當理由，等於把自己的錢交給別人的判斷，虧了還不知道該怪誰。你怕承認，自己拿別人的判斷當理由。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 No matter what, don't use the epilogue as your reason to buy bank stocks. You must strictly follow the book's methods, do thorough research, develop a complete investment and trading strategy, and execute buys and sells strictly—that's the right approach. The author's warning is: you can listen to opinions, but you must build the reasoning yourself—using "the author is bullish" as your reason is like handing your money over to someone else's judgment and not even knowing who to blame when you lose. You're afraid to admit you use others' judgment as your reason.

qa.q: 「股指期貨的避險功能必將成為做多中國股市的一劑興奮劑」——制度變化來臨時，你提前研究過嗎？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 股指期貨成為資本市場重大事件，藍籌股將進一步受到大資金關照，其避險功能必將成為做多中國股市的一劑興奮劑。制度變化的影響，早在正式落地前就開始發酵——你總等「落地了」才反應，而那個時候，聰明錢已經佈局完畢。你怕承認，自己總等落地了才反應。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 Stock index futures becoming a major event in the capital market means blue-chip stocks will get even more attention from big money, and their hedging function is bound to become a shot of adrenaline for going long on the Chinese stock market. The impact of institutional changes starts fermenting long before it officially lands—you always react after it's "landed," and by then, smart money is already positioned. You're afraid to admit you always react after the fact.

qa.q: 「存銀行喫負利息，不如買銀行股」——這個建議是給「沒風險承受能力的人」的，你覺得自己屬於這類人嗎？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 面對基礎物價上漲，把錢存進銀行喫負利息，還不如直接買銀行股更為直接，因為買銀行股可借金融精英之力實現資本增值。作者的建議建立在「銀行股風險相對可控」的判斷上——你聽到「不如買銀行股」就興奮，卻沒聽進去「這建議是給沒風險承受能力的人」；斷章取義，是散戶聽建議的常態。你怕承認，只聽半句。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 With basic prices rising, keeping money in the bank earning negative real interest is worse than directly buying bank stocks, because buying bank stocks lets you borrow the power of financial elites to grow your capital. The author's advice is based on the judgment that "bank stock risk is relatively manageable"—you get excited hearing "better to buy bank stocks" but miss that "this advice is for people with no risk tolerance"; taking things out of context is the norm when retail investors hear advice. You're afraid to admit you only listen to half.

qa.q: 你相信股價是「隨機」的，還是有一隻手在推？本書說那隻手是什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你看著一整屏股票齊齊翻紅，只當「行情來了」。一雙無形的手，本章將其定義為引導市場趨勢的主流資金；市場上股票走勢幾乎一致，正是主流資金作用的結果。你不去想誰有這本事，是怕一想就發現自己只是跟在後頭的——把齊漲當運氣，比承認被資金帶著走輕鬆。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 You see a whole screen of stocks turning green in unison and just think "the rally is here." An invisible hand—this chapter defines it as the mainstream capital that guides market trends; stocks moving almost identically is exactly the result of that mainstream capital at work. You don't want to think about who has that kind of power, because you're afraid you'd realize you're just trailing behind—treating the across-the-board rise as luck is easier than admitting you're being carried along by capital.

qa.q: 股價越跌，你越怕；資本卻越跌越進場——你與資本，誰更理性？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你那隻跌了三個月，慌得睡不著，資本卻正悄悄進場。資本總是向利潤大的方向流動。在資產淨值與未來盈利預期不變時，長期下跌使介入成本越來越低、利潤越來越大，資本的趨利避害特性便驅使資本漸漸流入。你越跌越怕、資本越跌越進，差的就是那點忍——你慌著割，它冷著撈。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 Your stock has been falling for three months, you're so panicked you can't sleep, but capital is quietly moving in. Capital always flows toward higher profits. When net asset value and future earnings expectations stay the same, a prolonged decline makes entry costs lower and lower and profits bigger and bigger, so capital's nature of seeking profit and avoiding loss drives it to gradually flow in. The more it falls, the more you panic; the more it falls, the more capital moves in—the difference is just a bit of patience. You panic and sell; it stays cool and scoops it up.

qa.q: 股票漲了很多之後，你是想「再加碼」，還是想「該跑了」？資本會怎麼做？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你那隻漲了很多，你卻捨不得賣，還想再衝一段。在資產淨值與未來盈利預期不變的情況下，股票長期上漲使介入成本越來越高，利潤相對越來越低，資本為追求更大利潤便會漸漸流出。你捨不得賣，是貪那口還沒到手的利潤——資本在撤，你還在等，等來的常是回吐。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 That stock of yours has gone up a lot, but you can't bear to sell—you want to ride it for one more stretch. If net asset value and future profit expectations stay the same, a long rally makes your entry cost higher and higher, and your relative profit thinner and thinner. Capital starts to trickle away, hunting for bigger gains. You won't let go because you're greedy for that profit that's still not in hand—capital's pulling out, and you're still waiting; what you usually end up with is giving all those gains back.

qa.q: 你追究「誰在操縱股價」，是想罵人，還是想搞懂規律？本書探討的目的是什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你虧了就愛罵「主力在操控」，從不想規律本身。目的在於讓人明白影響價格變動的那雙無形的手就是資本的流動規律，而非探究誰在控制主流資金、用什麼方法操縱股價。你死盯「誰在操控」，是圖有個能罵的人——你不是找規律，是在逃避承認那筆虧是自己下的單；推給主力，比承認看錯輕鬆。
keywords: 本書探討的目的是什麼
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 When you lose money, you love to curse 'the big players are manipulating,' without ever thinking about the rule itself. The point is to make you see that the invisible hand moving prices is just the law of capital flow—not to dig into who controls the mainstream money or what tricks they use to rig the market. You're so obsessed with 'who's manipulating' because you want someone to blame—you're not looking for the rule, you're avoiding the admission that you placed that losing trade yourself. Blaming the big players is a lot easier than admitting you read it wrong.

qa.q: 資本自己不會動——本書說它要流動，靠的是什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你總以為是「資金在進出」，其實每一筆進出背後，都有一個人在按鍵。資本要流動，需要通過人來實現；因此無論運作大資金還是小資金，運作資本的人必須尊重資本的流動規律。問題在於，人按鍵的那一刻，往往跟著貪和怕走，不跟著利潤走。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 You always think it's 'capital moving in and out,' but behind every single move, there's a person pressing the button. Capital needs people to move; so whether you're running big money or small money, you have to respect the law of capital flow. The thing is, the moment that person hits the button, they're usually following greed and fear, not following the profit.

qa.q: 如果你的錢有自己的「憲法」，第一條會是什麼？本書說資本運作者的第一條是什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你給自己的錢立過規矩嗎？多半沒有。資本的流動規律，即資本向利潤大的方向流動這一規律，是運作資本者奉行的最高、唯一的原則。你的規則裡缺這一條，是因為手癢總贏過原則——真立了「只流向利潤大處」，好多筆衝動的單當場就該砍掉。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 Have you ever set rules for your own money? Probably not. The law of capital flow—capital moves toward where the profit is bigger—is the highest and only principle for anyone who runs capital. Your rulebook is missing that exactly because your itchy fingers always beat your principles—if you actually set 'only go where the profit is,' a ton of those impulsive trades would've been cut right then and there.

qa.q: 股價長期下跌時，你看到的是「災難」，還是「成本變低」？本書教你用什麼眼光看？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你一看到大跌就血熱，只想「抄底」二字。應把漲跌理解為資本流動規律的外在表現：下跌使成本降低、利潤空間增大而引來資本，上漲使成本升高、利潤變小而逼走資本。你衝進去只為抄底，是貪那個低價的誘惑——真看懂利潤空間，你會等資本先動，而不是搶在它前頭。
keywords: 本書教你用什麼眼光看
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 The second you see a big drop, your blood starts pumping and all you can think is 'buy the dip.' You should understand the ups and downs as the outward look of the law of capital flow: a drop lowers costs, opens up more profit room, and attracts capital; a rally raises costs, shrinks profit, and forces capital out. You rush in just to catch the bottom because you're tempted by that low price—if you really understood profit room, you'd wait for capital to make the first move instead of jumping ahead of it.

qa.q: 為什麼熊市裡「所有股票一起跌」？本書說這是誰在起作用？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你挑股票，眼睛只釘著那一隻圖形。因為存在一雙影響甚至操縱股票價格變動的無形的手——引導市場趨勢的主流資金，它按資本流動規律整體運作，故股票走勢常趨一致。你捨不得先看整體資金，是怕抬頭看見大方向在退——隻盯個股，等於在退潮時挑哪朵浪好看。
keywords: 本書說這是誰在起作用
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 When you're picking stocks, your eyes are glued to that one chart. Because there's an invisible hand that influences or even manipulates stock price moves—the main force that guides the market trend. It operates as a whole according to the law of capital flow, so stocks often move in sync. You don't want to look at the overall capital first because you're afraid that if you look up, you'll see the big direction retreating—watching only your one stock is like picking which wave looks nicest as the tide goes out.

qa.q: 你買股票前，會把財務報表當成「聖經」嗎？本書說財務指標能當唯一依據嗎？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你把財務報表當聖經，報表漂亮就敢買。本章主張不要把財務指標作為買賣股票的唯一依據；財務指標雖重要，但企業好壞對股價影響微乎其微，股價變動主要受投資人對未來的判斷影響。你迷信報表，是貪那個「有依據」的安心——真虧了才發現，帳面好看的公司股價照跌。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 You treat financial reports like the Bible—if the numbers look good, you dare to buy. This chapter is all about not using financial indicators as the only reason to buy or sell a stock; they matter, sure, but whether a company is good or bad barely moves the stock price. Price changes are driven mainly by investors' expectations of the future. Your obsession with reports is just a craving for that 'I have a basis' comfort—when you actually take a loss, you realize a company with beautiful books can still see its stock fall just the same.

qa.q: 一家虧損累累的公司，股價為什麼能連漲？本書用什麼例子說明？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你買一隻虧損股卻連漲，百思不解。因為影響股價的主要因素是投資人對未來的判斷。例如一家經營不善、生產接近停止的公司，因被同行收購而重獲生機，股價反而連續上漲。你買的是「現狀」不是「想像」，是怕承認自己看的是過去——股價漲，漲在別人對未來的期待裡。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 You buy a stock that's losing money and it keeps going up, and you can't figure it out. That's because the main factor moving prices is investors' judgment about the future. For example, a company that's badly run and almost at a standstill can get a new lease on life when a rival buys it out, and its stock climbs instead. You're buying the 'current state' instead of the 'vision'—you're afraid to admit you're looking at the past. A stock rises on other people's hopes for the future.

qa.q: 等財報出爐再行動，會不會太遲？本書說財務指標有什麼致命弱點？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你抱著最新財報下單，覺得踏實。財務指標一年或一季才變動一次，相對股價變化滯後很多；等指標出爐，股價早已變動，無法作為即時買賣的依據。你信財報才動手，是貪那個遲來的安心——等報表出爐，行情早被跑在前頭的人走完，你只接到尾盤。
qa.a_en: Hey there! 😊 You place your order holding the latest earnings report, feeling solid. Financial indicators only change once a year or once a quarter, lagging way behind price movements. By the time the numbers come out, the stock price has already moved—they can't be used as real-time buy or sell signals. You trust the report before making a move because you're after that belated sense of security—by the time the report is out, the move's already been scooped up by those who got there first, and you're just catching the tail end.

qa.q: 同樣每股賺1元，股價卻能從10元漲到30元再跌回5元——本書用這個例子說明什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你那隻大起大落，翻遍財報卻找不到理由。以每股稅後利潤1元的股票為例：股價從10元漲到30元、又跌到5元，稅後利潤始終是1元不變，說明股價在不同時間變化並非因利潤變化所致。你硬從財報找原因，是不肯承認漲跌另有主因——賴在利潤上，比承認自己看不懂市場情緒輕鬆。
qa.a_en: Hey there! 😊 That stock of yours swings wild, but you scour the financial reports and can't find a reason. Take a stock with earnings per share of $1: the price goes from $10 to $30, then drops to $5, while earnings per share stays at $1 the whole time. That shows price changes over time aren't caused by profit changes. You're forcing a reason out of the report because you won't admit something else drives the swings—blaming it on profits is easier than admitting you can't read market sentiment.

qa.q: 財務指標不是沒用——本書說它正確的用途是什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你打開財報，眼睛只找「該買了」的證據。財務指標可以用來研究一家企業的發展趨勢，從而判斷這家企業股票未來的增值潛力，但不能單獨作為買賣信號。你把財報當買入藉口，是怕承認自己其實只想快點下單——真去研究趨勢，得花工夫，你捨不得。
qa.a_en: Hey there! 😊 You open the financial report, and your eyes are only looking for evidence that says "time to buy." Financial metrics can be used to study a company's development trend, and thus judge the stock's future growth potential, but they can't stand alone as buy or sell signals. You use the report as an excuse to buy because you're afraid to admit you just want to get the order in fast—really digging into trends takes effort, and you're not willing to spend it.

qa.q: 你覺得股價漲跌，反映的是「公司現在多好」，還是「大家覺得它未來多好」？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你買入只盯眼前數字，從沒想過市場怎麼看它。投資人預期企業未來轉好（如被收購後重獲新生），即使當前虧損累累、生產接近停止，股價仍會連續上漲，可見預期是股價變動的主導力量。你忽略預期，是貪那點看得見的數字——把「現在」當全部，等預期一變，帳面就翻臉。
qa.a_en: Hey there! 😊 When you buy, you only stare at the numbers in front of you, never thinking about how the market sees it. When investors expect a company to turn around (like being reborn after an acquisition), the stock can keep climbing even if the company is losing money and nearly halting production. That shows expectation is the dominant force behind price moves. You ignore expectations because you're greedy for the numbers you can see—you treat the "now" as everything, and when expectations shift, your paper gains turn on you.

qa.q: 當有人跟你說「好公司一定漲」，你該怎麼反駁？本書的證據是什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你看過好公司趴著、爛公司飛天，卻說不出道理。作者承認企業好壞集中表現在財務指標上，但強調企業好壞對股票價格影響微乎其微，並以虧損公司股價連漲為證，反駁唯財務指標論。你解釋不來，是死要面子——寧可罵市場瘋了，也不肯承認股價聽的是預期不是報表。
qa.a_en: Hey there! 😊 You've seen great companies flatline and junk companies fly, but you can't explain why. The author admits a company's quality is concentrated in its financial metrics, but stresses that quality has very little impact on stock price, using loss-making companies with rising share prices as proof, countering the idea that only financials matter. You can't explain it because you're too proud—you'd rather call the market crazy than admit the stock price listens to expectations, not the report.

qa.q: 你下一次買股票，會怎麼把財報和市場情緒放在一起用？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你買入前，報表看半天，預期和走勢卻沒進清單。先以財務指標研判企業發展趨勢與增值潛力，再結合投資人預期、股價走勢等動態因素決策，避免只看靜態報表就買賣股票。你冷落動態因素，是圖報表有憑有據——你抱報表不是為了看清楚，是為了給自己一個買的藉口；真算進預期走勢，你就得承認不該買。
qa.a_en: Hey there! 😊 Before you buy, you stare at the report for ages, but expectations and price trends don't make your checklist. First use financial metrics to assess a company's development trend and growth potential, then combine that with dynamic factors like investor expectations and price movement to decide—avoid trading solely on static reports. You leave out the dynamic factors because you want something concrete in the report—you hold onto that report not to see clearly, but to give yourself a reason to buy. If you really factored in expectations and trends, you'd have to admit you shouldn't buy.

qa.q: 利潤沒變，股價大起大落——這背後反映的是什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你買一隻，說不清買的是利潤還是預期。因為股價反映的是投資人對未來的預期與市場情緒，而非當下已實現的利潤；同樣1元利潤，股價可隨時間在不同價位大幅波動。你以為買的是利潤，其實多半買的是預期——怕承認自己押的是別人的想像，不是帳上的數。
qa.a_en: Hey there! 😊 You buy a stock but can't say whether you're buying profits or expectations. Because the stock price reflects investors' expectations and market sentiment about the future, not the profits already realized today. The same $1 profit can see the price swing wildly across different levels over time. You think you're buying profits, but really you're mostly buying expectations—you're afraid to admit you're betting on other people's imagination, not the numbers on the books.

qa.q: 你覺得決定股價的是股票本身，還是買賣股票的人？本書的答案是什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你打開軟體第一眼，總是先翻個股排行榜，找哪隻長得順眼。本章主張股票投資必須以人為本：研究股票投資首先必須研究人，因為人是市場的主體，是人的行為決定了股票價格走勢，而非股票本身。你盯著圖形研究股票，卻懶得研究圖形背後那羣人怎麼想；你怕承認，真正的盤不在K線上，在人的念頭裡。
qa.a_en: Hey there! 😊 The first thing you do when you open the trading app is scroll through the stock rankings, looking for one that looks good to your eye. This chapter argues that stock investing must be people-centered: to study stock investing, you must first study people, because people are the main players in the market, and it's human behavior that determines stock price movements—not the stocks themselves. You stare at charts and study the stock, but you can't be bothered to study what the people behind the charts are thinking. You're afraid to admit the real game isn't on the candlestick chart—it's in people's minds.

qa.q: 你會不會以為「以人為本」就是「市場圍著我轉」？本書怎麼糾正這個誤會？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你虧了一筆，第一反應是「這市場專門跟我作對」。不是。作者提醒切勿誤會「以人為本」等於市場以你為主，根本不是這回事；其真意是強調研究股票投資首先必須研究人，因為人是這個市場的主體。你之所以把以人為本聽成「以我為主」，是因為怪市場比怪自己容易；承認看不懂人，比認錯市場難得多。
keywords: 本書怎麼糾正這個誤會
qa.a_en: Hey there! 😊 You lost a trade, and your first thought is, "The market has it out for me." No, it doesn't. The author warns you not to misunderstand "people-oriented" as "the market revolves around me." That's not what it means at all. What it really means is that when you study stock investing, you must first study people, because people are the very subjects of this market. The reason you hear "people-oriented" as "me-oriented" is that blaming the market is easier than blaming yourself—and admitting you can't read people is way harder than admitting you were wrong about the market.

qa.q: 為什麼研究「人」比研究「股票」更重要？本書的依據是什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你看完一檔公司的財報，覺得「我懂這家公司了」，卻從沒想過誰在買賣它。因為人是這個市場的主體，股票價格走勢是由人的行為決定的，所以研究人比研究股票更為重要，研究重點應放在人身上。你花在鑽研圖表上的時間，遠多過花在琢磨人性上的；你捨不得把力氣給「人」，是怕一想就發現自己看不懂那羣對手。
qa.a_en: Hey there! 😊 You read a company's financial report and think, "I get this company now," but you've never once asked who's actually buying and selling it. Because people are the subjects of this market, and stock price movements are driven by human behavior, studying people matters more than studying stocks. The focus of your research should be on people. You spend way more time poring over charts than you do mulling over human nature. You won't give your energy to "people" because you're afraid that once you start thinking about it, you'll realize you can't read those opponents at all.

qa.q: 你會不會把自己的虧損歸咎於「指標不好用、軟體不給力」？本書說它們到底是什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你剛虧完，立刻去論壇搜「最好用的指標」，彷彿換把刀就能贏。這些都是次要的，都是工具，不是保證你賺錢的根本要素，不能指望依賴它們來保證盈利。你把虧損推給工具不好用，是怕承認問題出在自己手上；賴武器，比賴自己輕鬆。
keywords: 本書說它們到底是什麼
qa.a_en: Hey there! 😊 You just took a loss, and the very next thing you do is hit the forums searching for "the best indicator," as if switching knives will make you win. These are all secondary—they're just tools, not the fundamental factor that guarantees you money. You can't count on them to secure your profits. You blame the tools for your losses because you're afraid to admit the problem is in your own hands. Blaming the weapon is way easier than blaming yourself.

qa.q: 如果你只能靠一樣東西保證賺錢，你會選工具，還是選自己？本書的答案是？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你報了一堆課、買了一堆軟體，卻一年沒認真讀過一本關於自己的書。能夠保證賺錢的根本要素是人、是你自己。作者藉毛澤東「決定戰爭最終輸贏的是人而不是武器」來說明股市亦然，成敗繫於人而非工具。你寧可向外買「必勝武器」，也不肯花時間練自己這個要素；把錢砸在工具上，是怕承認真正該升級的是你。
qa.a_en: Hey there! 😊 You've signed up for a bunch of courses, bought a bunch of software, but you haven't seriously read a single book about yourself in a whole year. The fundamental factor that can guarantee profits is people—it's you. The author uses Mao Zedong's insight that "ultimately, what decides the outcome of a war is people, not weapons" to illustrate that the stock market works the same way: success or failure hinges on people, not tools. You'd rather buy "sure-win weapons" from outside than spend time training yourself—the real factor. Throwing money at tools is your way of dodging the truth that the one who really needs upgrading is you.

qa.q: 工具到底有沒有用？本書說好工具能做什麼、不能做什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你付款買下那套號稱「勝率九成」的軟體時，心裡莫名踏實了一下。好的工具只能讓股票投資賺錢更節省力氣、利潤更大，但它絕對不是保證你賺錢的主要因素，只是輔助手段。你買工具買的其實不是功能，是那份「這下不用再怕了」的安心；工具省的是力氣，省不掉你該做的判斷。
keywords: 本書說好工具能做什麼
qa.a_en: Hey there! 😊 When you paid for that software claiming a "90% win rate," you felt a weird sense of relief. A good tool can make stock investing more efficient and more profitable, but it is absolutely not the main factor that guarantees you profits—it's just a supporting aid. What you're actually buying with that tool isn't its function; it's that comforting thought: "Now I don't have to be scared anymore." Tools save you effort, but they can't save you from the judgment calls you still have to make.

qa.q: 股票投資是一場「不見硝煙的戰爭」——你的對手是誰？你的武器又是什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你帳面又綠了，第一個動作是打開App換個指標看，彷彿換武器就能翻盤。股票投資是不見硝煙的「戰爭」，同樣道理，決定你輸贏的是你自己而不是「武器」——即各種工具，這一點要刻骨銘心地記住。你總想靠升級裝備贏，是逃避承認真正決定輸贏的是握武器的那隻手；賴裝備，比認自己不行輕鬆。
qa.a_en: Hey there! 😊 Your portfolio's red again, and your first move is to open the app and switch indicators, as if changing weapons will turn things around. Stock investing is a "war" without gunpowder, and by the same logic, what decides whether you win or lose is you, not your "weapons"—meaning all those tools. Engrave this in your bones. You keep wanting to win by upgrading your gear because you're avoiding the truth that what really decides the outcome is the hand holding the weapon. Blaming your equipment is easier than admitting you're not good enough.

qa.q: 工具與人，誰是主、誰是從？本書的定位是什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你盯著別人曬的「神級指標」心癢，卻從沒問過那人本身賺不賺錢。武器只是工具，只能省力與放大利潤，不能保證賺錢；能保證賺錢的根本要素是人，人的因素永遠高於工具的因素。你迷信指標，是因為它聽起來有憑有據；真要你練自己，就得承認現在的自己還不夠格。
qa.a_en: Hey there! 😊 You see someone showing off their "god-tier indicator" and your fingers itch, but you've never once asked whether that person actually makes money. Weapons are just tools—they can save you effort and amplify profits, but they can't guarantee gains. The fundamental factor that guarantees profits is people. The human factor always outranks the tool factor. You're obsessed with indicators because they sound evidence-based. But if you really had to work on yourself, you'd have to admit that right now, you're just not good enough yet.

qa.q: 如果要你刻骨銘心記住一句話，你希望是哪句？本書要求記住的是哪句？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你每次輸錢，檢討清單上寫滿「指標鈍化、消息滯後」，唯獨沒有自己。要刻骨銘心記住：在股票投資這場不見硝煙的戰爭中，決定你輸贏的是你自己而不是武器，投資成敗的根本在於人。你把失敗歸給裝備，是死要面子不肯認；承認成敗在己，等於認了自己還得長進。
keywords: 本書要求記住的是哪句
qa.a_en: Hey there! 😊 Every time you lose, your post-mortem list is full of "indicators lagging" and "news was delayed," but yourself is never on it. Engrave this in your bones: in this war without gunpowder that is stock investing, what determines whether you win or lose is you, not your weapons. Success and failure in investing are rooted in people. You blame your equipment because you're too proud to admit the truth—admitting that success or failure rests on you means admitting you still have growing to do.

qa.q: 你未來的學習重心，該放在「人」還是「工具」上？本書的建議是什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你書架塞滿「擒莊祕笈」「指標大全」，卻沒一本教你讀懂自己。應把研究重點放在人（包括自己與市場參與者）身上，先研究人再研究股票，而不是一味依賴股票、指標或軟件等工具。你囤工具書，是貪那份「有方法就有了」的安心；真去讀人，得先承認自己還看不懂人。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 Your bookshelf is crammed with 'Secrets to Trapping the Big Money' and 'The Complete Guide to Indicators,' but not a single one teaches you how to read yourself. You should shift your focus to people—including yourself and the other players in the market. Study people first, then stocks, instead of relying purely on stocks, indicators, software, or whatever tool. The reason you hoard how-to books is that you crave the comfort of 'once I have the method, I'll be fine.' But truly reading people means first admitting you don't understand them yet.

qa.q: 你覺得自己虧錢，虧在「不懂方法」，還是「態度不對」？本書說要從哪裡開始？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你下單前心跳比思考快，事後卻說「我是看準才買的」。要從態度開始。因為投資人對相同信息的感受不同會導致行為不同，而憑情緒盲目下結論錯誤概率高，藉助工具理性判斷正確概率高，態度決定了判斷方式。你寧可說自己是方法不夠，也不肯認那筆是被情緒推著走；承認態度歪了，比學新方法難。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 Before you place an order, your heartbeat races ahead of your thinking, yet afterward you say, 'I bought because I saw it clearly.' It starts with your attitude. Because different investors can take in the same information differently, which leads to different actions—and jumping to conclusions on emotion has a high error rate, while using tools for rational judgment has a higher success rate. Attitude decides how you judge. You'd rather say your method isn't good enough than admit that trade was driven by emotion. Admitting your attitude is off is harder than learning a new method.

qa.q: 你的一次買入決定，可以拆成哪三個心理步驟？本書說它們怎麼遞進？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你一看到突破就按確認，連「為什麼買」都講不出一句完整的。三要素是認知、情感、行為。認知是對事物表面的認識，情感建立在認知基礎上產生心理體驗，行為是情感之後的結果，三者依次遞進。你每次衝動，都是情感搶在認知前頭；那一下手癢，讓行為跳過了思考這一環。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 The second you see a breakout, you hit confirm—you can't even string together a full sentence for 'why I bought.' The three elements are cognition, emotion, and behavior. Cognition is your surface-level understanding of something, emotion builds on that understanding to create a psychological experience, and behavior is the result after emotion. They go in that order. Every time you act impulsively, emotion cuts in line ahead of cognition. That itch in your fingers makes behavior skip the thinking step entirely.

qa.q: 同一隻股票、同一個價位，為什麼有人買有人賣？本書說差在哪裡？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你賣出的那一秒，總覺得對面那人是傻子，敢接你的貨。因為兩人對相同信息的感受不同：一個認為價格太高而賣出，另一個認為價格太低而買進，感受不同直接導致行為不同。你笑對手傻，是怕認真一想會發現自己纔是那個憑感覺的；逃避比較，就永遠站錯邊。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 The second you sell, you always feel like the person on the other side is an idiot for taking your goods. Because two people experience the same information differently: one thinks the price is too high and sells, the other thinks it's too low and buys. Different feelings directly lead to different actions. You laugh at the other guy for being clueless because you're afraid that if you really think it through, you might find out you're actually the one going on feelings. Dodging the comparison means you'll always stand on the wrong side.

qa.q: 你的投資錯誤，大多發生在「看錯資訊」，還是「情緒上頭」？本書說問題出在哪一環？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你明明看對了方向，卻在盤中手癢砍掉，事後罵自己「怎麼沒忍住」。主要出在情感環節。認知階段接觸第一手信息不會出錯，行為本身也無失誤，只有情感體驗過程容易因個人情緒而盲目得出結論。你賴資訊、賴運氣，就是不賴那一下情緒；承認敗在情感，比賴別的難受。
keywords: 本書說問題出在哪一環
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 You clearly called the direction right, but mid-session your hands get itchy and you cut it, then beat yourself up after with 'why couldn't I just hold?' It mainly comes down to the emotion stage. In the cognition stage, taking in firsthand info doesn't go wrong, and the action itself isn't flawed either—only the emotional experience process tends to jump to blind conclusions because of personal feelings. You blame the news, you blame luck, but you won't blame that wave of emotion. Admitting you lost to emotion hurts way more than blaming something else.

qa.q: 大家看到的新聞、K線都一樣，為什麼結果天差地別？本書說差在哪裡？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你和羣友看著同一張圖，卻得出一多一空兩個結論，還都覺得對方瞎。因為投資人所接觸到的表面信息幾乎都是一致的、相同的，認知只是對事物表面的認識，大家看到的信息相同，所以在認知階段不容易出錯。你以為差在資訊，其實差在「感受」；把分歧推給沒看全，是怕承認是你自己讀歪了。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 You and your group buddies stare at the same chart, but one of you says long, the other says short, and you both think the other person's blind. Because the surface info investors get is almost always identical—cognition is just recognizing the surface, and since everyone sees the same info, it's hard to mess up at the cognition stage. You think the difference is in information, but it's really in 'how it feels.' Blaming the split on not seeing the full picture is your way of avoiding admitting that you're the one who read it wrong.

qa.q: 賺錢的人與虧錢的人，面對同一張K線圖，差別在哪裡？本書的答案是什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你買賣全憑「感覺要漲」，卻從沒用任何工具驗證過那感覺。錯誤的人純粹出於個人情緒盲目得出結論，正確的人往往藉助某種工具做出理性判斷後再下結論，差別在於判斷時靠情緒還是靠工具。你愛用感覺，是因為它不用做功課，也替你躲開了「承認自己不夠格」那一刻；逃避判斷，比下功夫輕鬆。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 You buy and sell purely on 'it feels like it's going up,' but you've never once used any tool to verify that feeling. People who get it wrong purely jump to conclusions from personal emotion; people who get it right tend to use some kind of tool to make a rational judgment before concluding. The difference is whether you rely on emotion or tools when judging. You love going with feelings because it means you don't have to do the homework, and it also lets you dodge that moment of admitting 'I'm not qualified.' Avoiding judgment is easier than putting in the work.

qa.q: 你覺得「憑感覺」和「用工具」哪個贏面大？本書給的概率結論是什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你嘴上承認「我多半是憑感覺」，下一筆照樣閉眼衝。凡由個人情緒盲目得出的結論，發生錯誤的概率高一些；藉助工具和手段理性判斷後得出的結論，正確的概率則高一些。你願意認這筆，卻不肯認那一筆；把虧損算在運氣上，比承認自己靠感覺輕鬆。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 You admit out loud, 'I'm mostly going by feel,' then the very next trade you close your eyes and charge in again. Conclusions reached blindly from personal emotion have a higher chance of error; conclusions made after rational judgment with tools and methods have a higher chance of being right. You're willing to own that trade, but not the next one. Chalking your losses up to luck is way easier than admitting you're running on feelings.

qa.q: 你下一次買賣前，會先檢查自己的「態度」嗎？本書建議怎麼檢查？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你下單前從不問自己「我現在情緒穩嗎」，手指已經在確認鍵上。在買賣前先審視自己的態度：是否被情緒左右，是否只憑感覺下結論；應藉助技術指標等工具進行理性分析後再決定買進或賣出。你跳過這道自問，是貪那一下的暢快；真停下來審自己的態度，就要當場承認不穩。
qa.a_en: Hey there～😊 You never ask yourself “Am I emotionally stable right now?” before placing an order—your finger's already hovering over the confirm button. Before you buy or sell, take a good look at your own attitude: are you being carried away by emotions, or jumping to conclusions based on gut feeling? You should use tools like technical indicators to analyze rationally before deciding to buy or sell. You skip that self-check because you're chasing that little rush; if you actually stopped to examine your attitude, you'd have to admit right on the spot that you're not steady.

qa.q: 你一直以為貪婪恐懼是缺點嗎？本書說它們是什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你一虧錢，就罵自己「太貪、太怕」，彷彿這兩樣是毛病。本章主張貪婪與恐懼不是人性的弱點，而是人作為高級動物最優秀的品質，尤其在經濟領域更是如此；認為投資不賺錢都是因貪婪恐懼所致的說法是可笑的言論。你把虧損全算在貪懼頭上，是怕往深處找真正的錯；賴人性，比賴自己的判斷輕鬆。
qa.a_en: Hey there～😊 The moment you lose money, you beat yourself up for being “too greedy, too scared”—as if those two things are flaws. This chapter argues that greed and fear aren't weaknesses of human nature, but the finest qualities of humans as advanced animals, especially when it comes to the economy. The idea that you don't make money investing because of greed and fear is just laughable. You pile all your losses onto greed and fear because you're afraid to dig deeper for the real mistake—blaming human nature is way easier than blaming your own judgment.

qa.q: 如果全世界都沒有貪婪和慾望，經濟會怎樣？本書說貪婪有什麼用？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你買進後漲了一截，立刻後悔「早知道多買點」——那股不滿足，就是貪在推。貪婪讓經濟得以不斷地發展和提高；若人人都克服了貪婪、沒有了需求，世界將多麼可怕，沒有發展動力的經濟一定會極其蕭條。你怕承認自己其實缺的是用法，不是缺貪；把貪當敵人，反而不去想怎麼讓它生財。
qa.a_en: Hey there～😊 After you buy and it climbs a bit, you instantly regret it—“Should've bought more.” That little itch of dissatisfaction? That's greed pushing you. Greed is what keeps the economy growing and improving; if everyone overcame greed and had no needs, how terrifying would the world be? An economy with no driving force would be utterly depressed. You're afraid to admit that what you're actually missing is the know-how, not the greed. By treating greed as the enemy, you never think about how to make it work for you.

qa.q: 你怕虧錢，是懦弱還是本能？本書說恐懼有什麼用？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你被深套後，反而奇蹟似地鎮定，連止損都懶得想。恐懼讓人們學會了許多保護自己的手段；人若失去了恐懼的本能，也就意味著失去了自我保護的意識，那麼人類能否繼續生存都將值得懷疑。你那種「不怕了」，其實是麻痺；真要你承認還在怕，就得面對自己沒設好防線。
qa.a_en: Hey there～😊 When you're deeply trapped in a position, you strangely calm down—you can't even be bothered to think about a stop-loss. Fear taught humans so many ways to protect themselves; if people lost their instinct for fear, they'd also lose their sense of self-preservation, and whether humanity could even keep surviving would be questionable. That “I'm not scared anymore” of yours is really just numbness. If you truly admitted you're still scared, you'd have to face the fact that you never set up your defenses.

qa.q: 什麼時候你該「越貪婪越好」？本書給的時機是什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 牛市裡你賺了點就跑，看它繼續噴就捶桌，卻不敢再上車。在大牛市中，趨勢多頭走勢良好，此時一定要貪婪，越貪婪越好，這樣能把利益最大化，把優良的品質轉化為財富。你不是不貪，是怕貪錯；可牛市的規矩偏偏要你敢貪，你那一下退縮，把該賺的還給了市場。
qa.a_en: Hey there～😊 In a bull market, you take a small profit and run, then watch it keep ripping upward and slam the table—but you don't dare get back in. In a major bull market, the trend is strong and healthy—this is exactly when you need to be greedy, the greedier the better, so you can maximize your gains and turn that fine quality into wealth. It's not that you're not greedy—you're afraid of being greedy wrong. But the rule of a bull market is that you have to dare to be greedy, and that one moment of hesitation? You handed the money you should've made right back to the market.

qa.q: 什麼時候你該「越膽小越好」？本書說恐懼的正確用法是什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 熊市連跌，你卻把倉位抱得死緊，嘴裡唸「總會回來的」。在大熊市中，趨勢走勢空頭，此時一定要恐懼，越膽小越好，這樣才能保證自己的資金安全，善用恐懼這一自我保護的本能。你以為那叫「扛」，其實是怕承認該恐懼；真恐懼，你早就把資金護住了。
qa.a_en: Hey there～😊 In a bear market, everything keeps falling, but you hold your position like it's glued to your hands, muttering “it'll come back eventually.” In a major bear market, the trend is bearish—this is exactly when you need to be fearful, the more timid the better, so you protect your capital and put that self-protective instinct of fear to good use. You think that's “holding strong,” but really you're afraid to admit you should be scared. If you were truly fearful, you'd have protected your money long ago.

qa.q: 貪婪和恐懼本身沒有對錯——本書說用什麼來引導它們？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你漲時貪、跌時更貪抄底，完全不管現在是多是空。用趨勢來引導恐懼和貪婪向正確的方向發展是最為科學的方法，即順應趨勢方向決定何時該貪婪、何時該恐懼。你的貪懼是跟著帳面走的，不是跟著趨勢；賴情緒，是因為看清方向要下功夫，你捨不得。
qa.a_en: Hey there～😊 When it's going up, you're greedy; when it's falling, you're even greedier catching the knife—you don't care at all whether the trend is up or down. Using the trend to guide fear and greed in the right direction is the most scientific approach: follow the trend to decide when to be greedy and when to be fearful. Your greed and fear follow your account balance, not the trend. You blame your emotions because seeing the direction clearly takes real work, and you're just not willing to put it in.

qa.q: 專家說「投資虧錢都是貪婪恐懼害的」——本書怎麼看這種說法？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你聽專家說「戰勝貪恐才能贏」，連連點頭，轉頭照舊追漲殺跌。專家們把貪婪和恐懼當作人性的弱點來大加批判，得出投資股票不賺錢都是因為貪婪和恐懼所致的近乎偏執的結論，作者認為這是多麼可笑的言論。你拿這句當遮羞布，把虧損全推給人性；不肯看真正的問題，是怕那問題長在自己身上。
qa.a_en: Hey there～😊 You hear experts say “conquer greed and fear and you'll win,” and you nod along—then the next second you're back to chasing rallies and dumping on dips. Experts love to trash greed and fear as weaknesses of human nature, concluding with almost paranoid stubbornness that losing money in stocks is all because of greed and fear. The author thinks that's just ridiculous. You use that line as a fig leaf, pushing all your losses onto human nature. You won't look at the real problem, because you're afraid it might be living right inside you.

qa.q: 要把貪婪恐懼用對地方，前提是解決什麼問題？本書接下來要做什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你聽了一百遍「別貪別怕」，可真到盤中，那兩個字半點用都沒有。作者表示後面將有一攬子的計劃來幫助讀者正確地解決趨勢的問題，為本書後續章節的具體方法埋下伏筆。貪懼本身不是毛病，看不清方向還硬做纔是；你賴自己心態差，是怕承認連趨勢都說不準。
keywords: 要把貪婪恐懼用對地方
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 You've heard "don't be greedy, don't be scared" a hundred times, but when it's actually in the middle of trading, those two words are completely useless. The author says there's a whole batch of plans ahead to help readers properly tackle the trend problem, foreshadowing the specific methods in later chapters. Greed and fear aren't the issue themselves; it's not being able to see the direction clearly and still forcing trades. You blame your own mentality as weak, but you're actually afraid to admit you can't even predict the trend.

qa.q: 你覺得投資成敗，關鍵在股票還是人？本書的答案是？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你又虧了，第一反應是「這隻股不行」，立刻找下一隻換。本章主張人的因素遠比股票自身更重要。作者以曾經滄海者自況，強調理念是先解決人的問題，人的心態與修養擺正後，剩下的投資問題自然迎刃而解。你寧可怪股票，也不肯怪自己；承認問題在「人」，等於認了自己還沒擺正。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 You lost again, and your first reaction is "this stock is no good," then you immediately start hunting for the next one. This chapter says the human factor matters way more than the stock itself. The author, as someone who's been through the wringer, stresses that the idea is to fix the person first—once your mindset and attitude are in the right place, the remaining investing issues just fall into place. You'd rather blame the stock than blame yourself; admitting the problem is in the "person" means admitting you haven't gotten yourself together.

qa.q: 你敢不敢算一算：兩年前賣掉的股票，如果拿到現在值多少？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你去年砍掉的那隻，今年打開一看漲了三倍，當場想把App卸了。因為任何被賣掉的股票，若能有足夠耐心持有至今，早已是百萬或千萬富翁。回憶在於提醒讀者：我們常因缺乏足夠的耐心而與財富失之交臂。你寧可怪自己手賤，也不肯承認那是缺耐心；承認「再忍忍就好」，比承認看不懂難受。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 The stock you cut last year—you open your app this year and see it's tripled, and you almost delete the app on the spot. Because any stock you sold, if you'd just had enough patience to hold it till now, you'd already be a millionaire or even a multi-millionaire. This memory is here to remind you: we often lose wealth because we don't have enough patience. You'd rather blame your own itchy hands than admit it's a patience problem; saying "I should've just held on" hurts more than admitting you don't understand.

qa.q: 你為什麼拿不住一隻股票？本書說第一個原因是什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你手裡那隻橫盤三個月，你每天盯得心煩，恨不得馬上換掉。是對股票瞭解的程度不夠，看不到希望，自然就缺乏足夠的耐心。瞭解不深、看不到前景，是無法長期持有一隻股票的原因之一。你拿不住，是怕承認自己根本不懂它；把原因推給「股不行」，比承認無知輕鬆。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 That stock in your hands has been sideways for three months, and you stare at it every day, getting so annoyed you're itching to swap it out. It's because you don't know the stock well enough—when you can't see the hope, you naturally run out of patience. Not understanding it deeply, not seeing the potential, that's one of the reasons you can't hold a stock long-term. You can't hold on because you're scared to admit you just don't get it; blaming the "stock being no good" is way easier than owning up to your ignorance.

qa.q: 「想了解卻無從下手」——這種無知，本書說怎麼補救？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你想搞懂持倉股，打開財報卻像看天書，翻兩頁就關掉。更重要的原因之一是無知，想要更多地瞭解股票卻無從下手。因此正確掌握必要的專業知識，是培養耐心的重要途徑。你說「想學但沒門路」，其實是怕一學就照出自己的空；躲開專業，耐心永遠長不出來。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 You want to figure out your holdings, but opening the financial report is like reading some ancient secret script—you flip a couple pages and close it. A bigger reason is ignorance: you want to learn more about the stock but have no clue where to start. So getting a solid grip on the necessary know-how is an important path to building patience. You say "I want to learn but I don't have a way in," but really you're afraid that once you start learning, it'll shine a light on how empty your knowledge is; if you dodge the professional stuff, patience will never grow.

qa.q: 別人的股票漲得比你的多，你就想換股——這說明你缺什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 羣友曬出翻倍單，你盯著自己的龜速股，手已經癢著想換。修養不夠、個人品質不好是沒有耐心的另一主要因素。看到別人的股票漲得比自己的多，內心產生深深的不平衡心理，便失去了應有的耐心。你輸的不是股，是那股不平衡；不肯認自己是被別人帶偏的，是怕承認修養還不夠。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 Someone in the group shows a screenshot of their stock doubling, and you stare at your turtle-paced stock, fingers already itching to switch. Not having enough self-cultivation and poor personal character are the other big reasons for lacking patience. When you see someone else's stock rising more than yours, a deep feeling of unfairness kicks in, and you lose the patience you should have. What you're losing to isn't the stock—it's that imbalance; you refuse to admit others swayed you because you're scared to acknowledge your own character still needs work.

qa.q: 耐心不是硬撐出來的——本書說怎麼才能「自然地」拿得住？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你對持倉股的前景，全靠「應該會漲吧」這句撐著，從沒算過為什麼。藉助一種工具對股票有深刻的瞭解，從而看到未來的希望；多一些平常心，像強者一樣思考問題，以同情和寬慰的胸懷為人處事。你貪那個「希望」的感覺，卻不肯下功夫真弄懂；把幻想當希望，比承認沒底輕鬆。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 For your holdings, your hope for the future is carried entirely by "it should go up, right?"—you've never actually worked out why. If you use a tool to really know the stock deeply, then you can see the hope ahead; add a little equanimity, think like a big shot, handle things with empathy and a calming heart. You're hooked on that "hope" feeling, but you won't grind to truly understand—taking fantasy as hope is way easier than admitting you're groundless.

qa.q: 「像強者一樣思考」具體是什麼意思？本書怎麼解釋？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 別人帳面紅通通，你那隻原地踏步，你整晚刷著別人的曬單睡不著。指不因他人股票上漲而心生失衡，像大人物一樣為人處事，保持平常心看待漲跌，專注於自己持有股票的價值與未來的希望。你心煩，是因為把別人的漲跌當成了自己的輸贏；承認被帶節奏，比裝淡定難。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 Everyone else's accounts are all nice and red, while yours is stuck in place, and you spend the whole night scrolling through their play-by-plays, unable to sleep. It means not getting unbalanced by other people's stock gains, acting like someone important, keeping a level head about ups and downs, and focusing on the value and future hope of your own holdings. You're anxious because you've turned their moves into your own wins and losses; admitting you're being led along is harder than just pretending to be chill.

qa.q: 「先解決人的問題」——具體先做哪兩件事？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你總問「有沒有不用學、直接拿結果的懶人法」。先修心：深入瞭解股票、掌握專業知識以看到希望，克服無知；再修養：以同情寬慰的胸懷剋制不平衡心理，用平常心耐心持有，問題自然迎刃而解。你貪那條捷徑，是怕承認得先補自己；真去修心修養，就得認現在的自己還空。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 You keep asking for a “lazy way to get results without studying.” First, work on your mindset: dig deeper into stocks, build real knowledge so you can see hope, and overcome ignorance. Then work on your character: hold back that jealous, unbalanced feeling with compassion and a generous heart, and hold your positions with patience and a calm mind—then the problems will just resolve themselves. The shortcut you're craving? It's because you're afraid to admit you need to fix yourself first. But to truly work on your mind and character, you have to admit that who you are right now just isn't enough yet.

qa.q: 你拿不住股票，屬於三類原因中的哪一類？本書列了哪三類？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你每次砍完又漲，都歸結成一句「我運氣不好」。一是對股票瞭解的程度不夠、看不到希望；二是無知、想多瞭解卻無從下手；三是個人品質不好、修養不夠，因別人股票漲得多而生不平衡心理。你賴運氣，是不肯把三類原因往自己身上套；承認是哪類，就等於認自己得改。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 Every time you cut your losses and the stock shoots up, you sum it up as “I just had bad luck.” First, you don't understand the stock well enough to see its potential. Second, you're in the dark—you want to learn more but don't know where to start. Third, there's a character issue—your cultivation isn't deep enough, so you get jealous when others make more. You blame luck because you won't put those three reasons on yourself. Admit which category it is, and you're basically admitting you need to change.

qa.q: 你虧錢後的第一反應，是「下次報仇」還是「總結原因」？本書說你需要什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你被洗出局那刻，滿腦子「這市場欠我一次」，盤後還在咬牙。主張投資者要有大海般的寬大胸懷。因為股票投資是大事情，斤斤計較者做不了大事；且股市傷害無針對性，無法報復，只有大度才能保持正常思維。你想報復卻找不到對象，是怕承認這口氣只能自己吞；賴市場，比認自己該大度輕鬆。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 The moment you got shaken out, all you could think was “the market owes me one,” and you were still grinding your teeth after hours. The advice is to have an ocean-wide, generous heart. Stock investing is a big game—petty people can't handle big things. And the market's blows aren't aimed at anyone personally, so there's no one to get revenge on. Only with a big heart can you keep a clear head. You want revenge but can't find a target—because you're afraid to admit that this frustration is yours to swallow. Blaming the market is easier than admitting you should be the bigger person.

qa.q: 什麼樣的人算「大度」？本書最簡單的解釋是什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你一虧就衝去羣裡訴苦，把經過講了三遍，卻沒靜下來想哪錯了。擁有大海一樣的寬大胸懷。一個大度的人能坦然面對挫折，平靜地尋找遭受挫折的原因，從而找出更好的辦法解決問題。你急著找人聽，是怕獨自面對那個錯；承認該平靜找原因，比發洩難。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 The moment you lose money, you rush to the group to vent, retell the story three times, but never sit quietly to think about what went wrong. Be someone with an ocean-wide, generous heart. A magnanimous person can face setbacks calmly, quietly look for the cause, and then find a better way to solve the problem. You're in a hurry to find someone to listen, because you're scared of facing that mistake alone. Admitting you should calmly find the cause is harder than just venting.

qa.q: 虧錢後越想越氣，會怎樣影響你後面的操作？本書說仇恨憤怒的代價是什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你虧了一筆，越想越氣，反手就加倉「討回來」，結果又喫一刀。人受傷害後陷入痛苦、圍繞報復打轉，仇恨和憤怒會讓一個人失去理智，從而失去對事物發展的正確認識態度，後來的機會因此白白失去。你賭氣操作，是怕那口氣咽不下去；可憤怒替你做的決定，從來沒好下場。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 You took a loss, the more you thought about it the angrier you got, so you doubled down to “win it back”—and got cut again. When you're hurt, you sink into pain and spin around revenge—hatred and anger make you lose your rationality, and with that, you lose the right perspective on how things are unfolding. So the opportunities that come later just slip away. You made that spiteful trade because you couldn't stand to swallow your pride. But decisions made in anger never end well for you.

qa.q: 現實中被欺負你可以報復，股市裡虧了錢你能找誰算帳？本書說差在哪裡？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你虧錢後盯著大盤罵莊家，彷彿有個具體的人該為你負責。現實中的傷害有對象，報復對手可舒緩情緒、得到快感；而股市投資招致傷害後往往沒有針對性，無法確定誰傷害了你，因此無法靠報復紓解情緒。你編了個「敵人」來恨，是怕承認傷害本無主；有對象可恨，比承認無處發洩輕鬆。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 After losing money, you stare at the market and curse the market maker—like there's this specific person who should be held responsible. When hurt in real life, there's a target for your pain—getting back at your rival can soothe you and give you some satisfaction. But with stock market investing, after you get hurt, there's usually no specific target—you can't pinpoint who hurt you, so revenge can't relieve your emotions. You made up an “enemy” to hate, because you're afraid to admit that the hurt had no owner. Having someone to hate is easier than admitting there's nowhere to direct your frustration.

qa.q: 如果情緒一直紓解不了，你的交易會變成什麼樣？本書說會失去什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你氣還沒消就又開了新倉，單子下得比平時更沖。無法得到報復的快感，情緒無法舒緩，將從此失去一個正常人應有的正常思維，進而影響判斷與決策。你捨不得讓情緒過夜，是貪那口立刻討回的爽；可帶著氣做決定，虧的總是你。
keywords: 如果情緒一直紓解不了
你的交易會變成什麼樣
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 You're still fuming when you open a new position, and the order hits harder than usual. When you can't get the thrill of revenge and your emotions can't be soothed, you'll permanently lose the normal thinking a normal person should have—and that will mess with your judgment and decisions. You won't let your emotions cool overnight because you crave that instant payback. But making decisions when you're angry? You're the one who always ends up bleeding.

qa.q: 股市裡有「智者和神經病」兩種人——你覺得自己更像哪一種？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你虧完就四處嚷嚷「股市都是騙局」，聽起來像個輸紅眼的人。股票市場最容易出現兩種人：一種是擁有財富的智者，另一種是失去財富的神經病；成為神經病還是智者，根本區別在於是否擁有大度的胸懷。你寧可當那個罵街的，也不肯練大度；承認自己正在變成神經病，比認輸還難堪。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 After losing, you go around shouting “the stock market is all a scam,” sounding like someone who's lost their mind. The stock market tends to breed two kinds of people: one is the wise person who has wealth, and the other is the lunatic who lost it. Whether you become a lunatic or a wise person comes down to whether you have a generous spirit. You'd rather be the one yelling in the street than practice being big-hearted. Admitting you're slowly turning into a lunatic is even more uncomfortable than admitting you lost.

qa.q: 大度是天生的嗎？本書說可以怎麼練出來？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你見誰虧了都忍不住嘲一句「活該」，從沒想過自己也在裡頭。從善良和同情心做起，適當地賦予弱者一些同情，從中得到精神上的快感，把自己擺在強者的位置，面對傷害時把傷害看作一種財富。你笑別人弱，是怕承認自己同樣會被市場教育；把同情給出去，等於認自己也會痛。
keywords: 本書說可以怎麼練出來
qa.a_en: Hey～😊 You see anyone lose money and can't help sneering "serves them right," never thinking you're in the same boat. Start with kindness and empathy, give the weak some compassion, get a little mental thrill from it, put yourself in the position of the strong, and when faced with harm, treat it as a kind of wealth. You laugh at others for being weak because you're afraid to admit the market can school you too; giving sympathy is admitting you can also hurt.

qa.q: 你願不願意把上一次的虧損當成「學費」，而不是「傷口」？本書說這樣做有什麼用？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你把每筆虧損都記成「仇」，帳本越寫越像一本怨氣錄。把傷害當作財富，不陷於報復與怨恨，慢慢就會擁有一個大度的胸懷，從而以正常思維面對市場，避免因情緒失控而損失更多。你捨不得翻篇，是怕那筆就這麼「白虧了」；可記著仇，虧的就不止是錢。
keywords: 本書說這樣做有什麼用
qa.a_en: Hey～😊 You log every loss as a "grudge," and your ledger starts reading more like a book of resentment. Treat harm as wealth, don't sink into revenge and bitterness, and gradually you'll develop a magnanimous heart—then you can face the market with a clear head and avoid losing even more from emotional spiral. You can't let it go because you're afraid that loss would've been "for nothing"; but holding a grudge means you lose more than just money.

qa.q: 面對虧損帶來的情緒，本書給的核心方法論是什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你下次再虧，第一件事多半還是先罵、先慌，而不是先想。以心態修養為方法：用大度化解股市虧損帶來的情緒傷害，坦然面對挫折、平靜分析原因，把挫折轉化為解決問題與積累經驗的財富。你總把情緒擺在最前，是貪那下發洩的暢快；真要先分析原因，就得忍住那股委屈。
qa.a_en: Hey～😊 Next time you lose, the first thing you'll probably do is still curse and panic, not think. Use mindset cultivation as your method: dissolve the emotional sting of market losses with magnanimity, face setbacks calmly, analyze the causes with a steady head, and turn setbacks into wealth of problem-solving and experience. You always put emotions first because you crave the rush of venting; if you truly analyzed the causes first, you'd have to hold back that bitterness.

qa.q: 選對股票和應對挫折，哪個更能決定你的結果？本書的答案是？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你選股越挑越準，一遇到回撤就全亂了陣腳，前面選對的全白費。主張很好地應對挫折，遠比買到一隻好股票更重要。因為挫折無處不在，能否妥善應對直接決定投資結果，而非僅靠選股。你花力氣選股，卻不肯練應對；承認輸在應對，比承認選股差難受。
keywords: 哪個更能決定你的結果
qa.a_en: Hey～😊 Your stock picking gets sharper and sharper, but the moment there's a pullback you fall apart, and all those good picks go to waste. Handling setbacks well matters far more than buying a good stock. Because setbacks are everywhere, and how well you handle them directly decides your investment outcome—not just stock selection. You put all your effort into picking stocks but refuse to practice handling; admitting you lose on the handling is harder than admitting your picks were bad.

qa.q: 「買了就跌、賣了就漲」——這種事你遇到過幾次？本書說這算什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你賣掉沒兩天就飆，你坐在螢幕前捶桌，覺得全世界在跟你作對。看好的股票買入後不漲反跌是挫折；忍無可忍砍掉之後該股卻連續上漲也是挫折。凡是需求未能被滿足的行為都屬於挫折的範疇。你把「賣了就漲」當成運氣背，是怕承認那也是自己應對的一部分；賴命，比認自己輕鬆。
qa.a_en: Hey～😊 You sell and it soars two days later, and you're pounding the desk thinking the whole world is against you. Buying a stock you're confident in and watching it fall instead of rise is a setback; enduring it until you can't anymore, cutting it, and then watching it climb steadily is also a setback. Any unmet need falls under the category of setbacks. You call "it goes up after I sell" bad luck because you're afraid to admit that's part of your process too; blaming fate is easier than blaming yourself.

qa.q: 挫折真的可怕嗎？本書說真正可怕的是什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你一綠就到處問「要不要砍」，問完更慌，手忙腳亂把單亂點一通。因為真正糟糕的是遭受挫折之後手忙腳亂，沒有相應的策略來處理，從而使結果變得更加糟糕，而不是挫折事件本身。你怕承認自己沒預案，才會在事發時亂；賴事件太突然，比認自己沒準備輕鬆。
qa.a_en: Hey～😊 The moment it turns red you run around asking "should I cut?" and end up more panicked, frantically clicking orders. Because what's truly bad is scrambling after a setback with no strategy to handle it, making things worse—not the setback itself. You're afraid to admit you don't have a plan, so you scramble when it happens; blaming it on "too sudden" is easier than admitting you weren't prepared.

qa.q: 你虧錢後，會把原因歸給「大環境」還是「自己」？本書說原因分哪兩類？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你虧了先嘆「大環境太差」，把帳全算給外面，自己乾乾淨淨。一種是客觀因素造成，屬於人力不可抗拒；另一種是主觀因素造成，屬於個人努力的程度不夠，後者是不可原諒且需要反省的。你把客觀當盾牌，是怕扒開看主觀那層；承認有幾成是自己，比賴大盤難。
qa.a_en: Hey～😊 When you lose, you first sigh "the market's just too bad," piling all the blame on the outside and keeping yourself clean. Some setbacks are caused by objective factors—beyond human control; others are caused by subjective factors—insufficient personal effort. The latter is unforgivable and needs reflection. You use objective factors as a shield because you're afraid to dig into the subjective layer; admitting part of it was on you is harder than blaming the market.

qa.q: 當挫折是自己造成的，本書說該用什麼態度對待？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你檢討到最後，總用「下次注意」收尾，轉頭就原諒了自己。屬於不可原諒、非常需要反省的挫折，因為問題出在個人努力與投資策略上，可以通過改進自己來避免重蹈覆轍。你捨不得真反省，是怕那句話戳破自己；原諒自己，比改自己容易。
qa.a_en: Hey～😊 When you finish reviewing, you always wrap it up with "I'll be careful next time," then immediately forgive yourself. That's the unforgivable kind of setback that really needs reflection, because the problem lies in personal effort and investment strategy, which can be fixed by improving yourself to avoid repeating the same mistake. You can't bring yourself to truly reflect because you're afraid that sentence will pierce through you; forgiving yourself is easier than changing yourself.

qa.q: 牛市裡頻繁進出反而虧錢——本書說這是誰的責任？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 牛市裡你天天進出，賺點就跑、跌了就補，忙得很有成就感。因為牛市的正確策略是長期持股、讓利益最大化；頻繁操作是策略不當，又沒有及時改正，虧損純粹由主觀因素造成。你愛那種「我在操作」的充實，是手癢；真長期抱著，就得忍住不看盤的慌。
qa.a_en: Hey there～😊 In a bull market, you're in and out every day—grab a little profit and run, buy the dip, and it keeps you busy and feeling accomplished. But the right strategy in a bull market is to hold long-term and let profits run; overtrading means your strategy's off, and if you don't fix it in time, the losses are purely on you. That feeling of “I'm doing something” you love? That's just itchy hands. Truly holding long-term means fighting the urge to check the market and panic.

qa.q: 喫一塹之後，怎麼纔算真的「長一智」？本書說總結之後要做什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你說「下次不追高了」，第二天看見異動照追，教訓半句都沒留下。需要反省自己的投資策略，找出策略不當之處，並為後來制定投資策略積累經驗，避免重犯同樣的錯誤。你以為自己在總結，其實只是在重複一次不甘；不甘撐不過開盤，規則才撐得過。
qa.a_en: Hey there～😊 You say “I won't chase the next spike,” but the next day you see a move and you're right back at it—not a single lesson learned. You need to reflect on your investment strategy, figure out where it went wrong, and use that to build a better plan going forward so you don't repeat the same mistakes. You think you're summing things up, but really you're just replaying your frustration; frustration won't survive the opening bell—rules will.

qa.q: 虧損發生的那一刻，你第一個動作應該是什麼？本書的順序是什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你虧完總想「先睡一覺再說」，結果拖到週末才肯動筆想。首先要做的就是及時分析導致挫折的原因，並在第一時間制定應對策略，盡可能地降低因為挫折帶來的損失。你拖著不分析，是怕那個原因長在自己身上；晚一刻面對，就多一刻躲著。
qa.a_en: Hey there～😊 You always think “I'll just sleep on it first” after a loss, and then you put off actually analyzing it until the weekend. The first thing to do is analyze what caused the setback in a timely manner, then act on it immediately to minimize the damage. You're putting off the analysis because you're afraid the cause might be on you; every moment you delay facing it, you're hiding a little longer.

qa.q: 如果有人問你「你在股市混了多久、學過什麼」，你能用一個數字證明自己嗎？本書用什麼作為唯一的評價標準？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你逢人愛聊自己「炒了幾年股」，卻不提帳戶是紅是綠。投資股票的唯一目的就是賺錢；不管投身股市多久、有無經驗、是專家還是新手，只要能賺錢，一切纔有意義，不能賺錢則一切都免談。資歷是裝飾，結果纔是答案。你拿資歷撐面子，是因為結果拿不出手；帳戶不會陪你演，它只認賺沒賺。
qa.a_en: Hey there～😊 You love telling people you've “been trading for years,” but never mention whether your account is in the red or green. The only goal of investing in stocks is to make money; no matter how long you've been in the market, whether you're experienced or a newbie, expert or amateur—if you're making money, it all matters; if you're not, nothing else does. Seniority is decoration; results are the answer. You rely on seniority to save face because your results can't stand up to scrutiny; your account isn't going to put on an act with you—it only cares if you've made money.

qa.q: 你會不會也常聽失敗者高談闊論，聽完還覺得很有道理？本書說這種談話有什麼危害？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你愛聽羣友大談虧錢血淚，聽完還覺得「有共鳴」。因為虧錢的經驗沒有指導價值，反覆談論失敗經驗只會把錯誤觀念傳播給更多人，對聽者的危害越大，所以不如不談。失敗的故事動聽，卻會讓聽的人照著再輸一次。你聽的是故事，染上的是觀念；把別人的錯當共鳴，不過是想躲進人羣裡逃避承認：輸的那個其實是你自己。
qa.a_en: Hey there～😊 You love listening to group members go on about their tearful losing streaks, and afterward you feel so “relatable.” But losing experience has no instructional value—rehashing failures just spreads the same wrong ideas to more people, and the more it's talked about, the more harm it does. So better not to talk about it at all. Failure stories sound compelling, but they make listeners go out and lose again exactly the same way. You hear a story, but you catch the mindset; mistaking someone else's mistakes for shared ground is just hiding in a crowd to avoid admitting: the one who lost is actually you.

qa.q: 你選「老師」時，看的是他的頭銜，還是他的帳戶？本書用什麼標準衡量專家？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你拜某「名師」為師，看的是他滿牆證照與頭銜。不賺錢的專家算不上專家；在股票市場上，只要能賺錢，即便是文盲也比不賺錢的學者價值更高，以賺錢與否作為唯一評價標準。頭銜不能替你扛虧損。你迷頭銜，是怕真去一問——承認自己可能看走了眼，比守住對名師的那份信任難得多。
qa.a_en: Hey there～😊 You're taking some “master” as your mentor, drawn by his wall full of certificates and titles. An expert who doesn't make money isn't an expert; in the stock market, as long as you're making money, even an illiterate person is worth more than a scholar who doesn't. Making money is the only metric. Titles won't take losses for you. You cling to titles because you're afraid to actually ask—admitting you might have backed the wrong horse is way harder than keeping your faith in that master.

qa.q: 你會不會用「長期投資」「價值發現」這些詞，給自己的虧損穿上外衣？本書說這件外衣是什麼做的？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你虧了一筆，脫口就是「這叫價值投資」，聽起來體面。因為股市以賺錢為唯一標準，沒有辦法用華麗的外衣讓它看起來高尚，而這件華麗外衣本身就是用「鈔票」做出來的，掩蓋不了虧損。再美的說法，也蓋不住帳戶的數字。你急忙披上漂亮說法，是為了面子不塌；可帳戶的數字，從來不認那件外衣。
keywords: 給自己的虧損穿上外衣
