qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 朋友問起近況，你說「還行，小賺」——帳戶其實是綠的。是虛榮。虛榮是除憤怒之外另一種傷害投資的情緒，隱藏較深、看似溫和，傷害卻是長期、深刻的，投資者必須正視並克服。它之所以難治，是因為每一次說出口，都能換來一陣很便宜的安慰。
keywords: 還有一種情緒傷你更深
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 When friends ask how you're doing, you say "pretty good, made a little"—but your account is actually in the red. That's vanity. Vanity is another emotion that hurts your trading, second only to anger. It's hidden deeper and seems milder, but the damage is long-term and profound—investors have to face it and overcome it. It's so hard to cure because every time you say it out loud, you get a cheap little hit of comfort in return.

qa.q: 憤怒像火，燒完就滅；虛榮像什麼？為什麼它比憤怒更難治？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 憤怒發完你自己都記得，虛榮卻連你自己都騙得過。虛榮是隱藏比較深的情感體驗，不像憤怒那樣極端明顯；虧損者不願承認虧損，長期掩蓋過失，缺乏別人的監督與外界刺激，永遠無法改過自新。看不見的傷，最難癒合——因為那點面子從來不痛，你也就從來不覺得該治。
keywords: 為什麼它比憤怒更難治
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 When you're angry, you at least remember it afterwards, but vanity can fool even yourself. Vanity is a deeper, more subtle emotional experience—not as extreme or obvious as anger. Losers won't admit they're losing, they cover up their mistakes for a long time, and without anyone holding them accountable or any outside push, they'll never change. Invisible wounds are the hardest to heal—because that pride never hurts, so you never feel like it needs treating.

qa.q: 虧了錢還吹自己賺了，說久了會怎樣？書裡說最後連誰都會被騙？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 那筆「賺了三成」你講了兩年，帳單早就找不到了。這樣的做法實際掩蓋了自身過失，時間長了會慢慢接受虧損的結果；謊言說多了，自己還以為真的就是那個賺錢的人，不僅不反省還愛炫耀——最後騙到的，是你自己。講第二次是面子，講第十次，是你真的信了。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 That "I made 30%" trade you've been talking about for two years—the trade confirmation is long gone. This kind of behavior actually hides your mistakes, and over time, you slowly start accepting the losses as okay. Say the lie enough times, and you actually start believing you're the one who made money. Not only do you stop reflecting, you start bragging—but in the end, the only one you're fooling is yourself. The second time you tell it, it's for pride. The tenth time, you genuinely believe it.

qa.q: 謊言說一百遍會變成什麼？為什麼缺乏監督的你，特別容易被自己騙？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你不記帳，所以「戰績」由嘴巴保管。反覆吹噓會讓自己產生錯覺，加上缺乏別人的監督以及外界因素的刺激，久而久之便接受了虛假的賺錢形象，永遠不會改過自新。沒有鏡子照著，謊言就成了真相——你不記帳，不是懶，是怕；記下來就得天天看見那個數字。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 You don't keep records, so your "track record" lives in your mouth. Repeated bragging creates an illusion, and combined with a lack of outside accountability and external triggers, you eventually accept a fake image of yourself as a profitable trader—and you'll never change for the better. With no mirror to reflect the truth, the lie becomes reality—you don't keep records not because you're lazy, but because you're scared. If you wrote it down, you'd have to look at that number every single day.

qa.q: 「虧錢成為習慣」是什麼意思？你怎麼知道自己有沒有走上這條路？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你已經不太去算今年的總帳了，連軟體都不太敢開。意味著你已無法正視錯誤、不再反省改進，自己還以為真的在賺錢；當虧錢成為習慣時，投資生涯基本上也就結束了。不敢開軟體的那幾秒，你不是在忙，是在逃避。
qa.a_en: Hey there! 😊 You've pretty much stopped tallying up the year's total, you can barely even bring yourself to open the software. That means you can't face your own mistakes anymore, you're not reflecting or improving, and you still think you're actually making money. When losing money becomes a habit, your investing career is basically over. Those few seconds when you don't want to open the software—you're not busy, you're avoiding.

qa.q: 虧了就是虧了——這句話你敢對自己說嗎？說完之後呢？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 說出「這筆我虧了」那六個字，比虧錢本身還難。實事求是，虧損了就是虧損了，勇於承擔自己的責任，把失敗當作改過自新的動力，而不是掩飾損失，讓虛榮心傷害金錢。你繞的那麼大一圈，護的從來不是錢，是面子。
qa.a_en: Hey there! 😊 Saying the words "I lost on this trade" is harder than the loss itself. Be realistic—a loss is a loss. Own up to your responsibility, treat failure as fuel to turn over a new leaf, instead of covering up your losses and letting vanity mess with your money. That whole big detour you took? It was never about protecting your money—it was about protecting your ego.

qa.q: 書裡那位「虧了還吹自己賺了多少」的投資人，你身邊有嗎？鏡子裡有嗎？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 聚會上總有一個人講得最響、帳戶最綠——你笑他，心裡卻有點坐不住。一位投資人虧損後一直不願承認虧損，總是誇誇其談吹噓自己賺了多少；看似無關緊要，實則掩蓋了過失，導致長期無法改過自新。你笑得越大聲，往往越像。
keywords: 虧了還吹自己賺了多少
qa.a_en: Hey there! 😊 At every gathering there's always that one person talking the loudest with the reddest account—you laugh at him, but deep down you feel a little uneasy. An investor who keeps refusing to admit his losses after losing, always boasting about how much he made. Seems harmless, but it's really just masking his mistakes, which keeps him from ever truly changing. The louder you laugh, the more you sound like him.

qa.q: 憤怒和虛榮，哪個更危險？作者為什麼把兩章放在一起講？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你替自己定過「不生氣下單」的規矩，卻沒定過「不吹牛」。兩者是並列補充：除憤怒這種極端情緒會傷害投資外，虛榮這種隱藏較深的情感同樣招致損失，且傷害更溫和而長期深刻。一明一暗，都是天敵——你只防看得見的那個，是因為看不見的那個，說破了很傷面子。
qa.a_en: Hey there! 😊 You made yourself a rule: "No placing orders when angry." But you never made one for "No bragging." The two go hand in hand: besides extreme emotions like anger that hurt your investing, there's a deeper hidden emotion like vanity that also causes losses—and its damage is gentler but far more lasting. One's obvious, one's hidden, but both are natural enemies—you only guard against the one you can see, because admitting the other one exists? That would sting your pride.

qa.q: 虛榮的傷害「看起來溫和」，為什麼反而是它最危險的地方？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你會替一次暴怒後悔，卻不會替一句吹牛後悔。因為虛榮是隱藏比較深的情感體驗，危害不像憤怒那樣顯而易見，所以表面溫和；但正是這種隱蔽性，使傷害變成長期、深刻的。它不痛，所以你從來沒把它當成敵人——這正是它最厲害的地方。
qa.a_en: Hey there! 😊 You regret a moment of rage, but you never regret a boast. Because vanity is a deeper, more hidden emotional experience—its harm isn't as obvious as anger, so on the surface it seems mild. But it's exactly that hidden nature that makes the damage long-term and profound. It doesn't hurt, so you never saw it as an enemy—and that's exactly why it's so powerful.

qa.q: 你上一次真心覺得「我還有東西要學」是什麼時候？作者為什麼把學習看得這麼重？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你看盤三小時，讀書三分鐘，還覺得自己一直在學。本章主張學習使人進步、活到老學到老；拒絕學習是股市虧損的重要根源，有追求的人不應拒絕任何學習機會。你不是沒時間讀書，是讀書太慢，慢到你得先承認自己還差得遠。
qa.a_en: Hey there! 😊 You stare at the charts for three hours, but only read for three minutes, and still think you're constantly learning. This chapter's point is that learning makes you better, and you're never too old to learn. Refusing to learn is a major root cause of losses in the stock market. Ambitious people shouldn't turn down any chance to learn. It's not that you don't have time to read—it's that you read so slowly, and slow enough that you first have to admit you're still far from where you need to be.

qa.q: 虧得越多越自負——這個「越」字，說的是別人還是你？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你最愛講的那筆，是三年前的事。自負者一直生活在過往的輝煌之中，對未來與現狀徹底失去信心，選擇逃避現實獲得短暫滿足，於是虧損與自負互為因果、形成惡性循環。虧損讓人害怕面對，害怕面對就只好嘴硬——你越講當年，越是不敢碰現在這張帳單。
qa.a_en: Hey there! 😊 The trade you love talking about most? That was three years ago. A conceited person keeps living in past glory, completely losing confidence in the future and the present, choosing to escape reality for a moment of satisfaction. So loss and arrogance feed each other, creating a vicious cycle. Loss makes you scared to face things, and when you're scared to face things, you get stubborn with words—the more you talk about back then, the less you dare to touch this bill in front of you now.

qa.q: 自負的根，書裡說是兩個字加兩個字——你知道是哪四個字嗎？你身上有嗎？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 看到別人貼對帳單，你嘴上說「運氣好」，眼睛卻盯了很久。無知、嫉妒。自負是無知、嫉妒共同作用的結果：對某件事情缺乏足夠知識去深刻了解，但是又不服氣別人的成績。那句「運氣好」，說出口的是不甘，不是判斷。
qa.a_en: Hey there! 😊 When you see someone else post their trade records, you say "lucky," but your eyes linger on it for a long time. Ignorance and envy. Arrogance is the result of ignorance and envy working together: you don't have enough understanding of something to really get it, but you can't stand someone else's results either. That "lucky" you say—what comes out is resentment, not a judgment.

qa.q: 別人賺5倍，你說「我做短線早賺10倍」——這句話你熟悉嗎？它暴露了什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 別人賺了五倍，你說「我要是做短線早十倍了」。自負最集中的表現是喜歡狡辯。例如別人長線持有獲利5倍，自負者會辯稱自己若做短線早能賺10倍，用想像中的成績貶低對方實際到手的利潤。那個「如果」不用成本也不用負責，所以它永遠比你帳戶裡的數字漂亮——你護的是面子，不是收益。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 Someone else made five times, and you say, "If I'd traded short-term, I'd already be up ten times." Arrogance really shows when you love to quibble. For example, when someone else holds long-term and gains 5x, the arrogant one argues they could've made 10x by trading short-term, using imaginary results to belittle the other person's actual profit. That 'if' costs nothing and doesn't need to be accountable, so it'll always look prettier than the number in your account—you're protecting your pride, not your returns.

qa.q: 想像中的10倍和到手的5倍，哪個更值錢？作者想讓你看清什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你腦子裡那個數字，比帳戶裡的好看十倍。別人的5倍是實實在在到手的利潤，自負者想像的10倍只是根據市場情況臆想、並非真正擁有，兩者有本質差別。投資講究以虧賺論英雄，想像中的利潤不是利潤——你捨不得放下那個數字，是因為放下就得承認自己還差得遠。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 That number in your head looks ten times better than the one in your account. Someone else's 5x is real profit in hand; the 10x you imagine is just a fantasy based on market conditions, not something you truly own—there's a fundamental difference. Investing rewards real gains and losses; imagined profit isn't profit. You can't let go of that number because letting go would mean admitting you're still far off.

qa.q: 「炒股就是賭博、學了也白學」——這句話是真理，還是拒絕學習的藉口？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 「炒股就是賭」這句話，你說了很多年。這是拒絕學習者找的藉口——認為投資靠運氣、聽消息，學了也是白學；作者以此點出此類心態正是放棄學習的錯誤根源。你愛這句話，是因為一旦成了賭，輸了就不必承認是自己不懂。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 You've been saying "trading stocks is just gambling" for years. That's the excuse people make when they refuse to learn—thinking investing is all luck and tips, so learning is pointless. The author points out that this attitude is exactly the wrong root cause of giving up learning. You love that saying because once it's a gamble, losing means you don't have to admit you actually don't understand.

qa.q: 自負的人為什麼學不進任何東西？他的耳朵和眼睛哪裡出了問題？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你問過別人「你用什麼指標」，卻沒問過「你怎麼看出來的」。自負者認為自己不需要學習，又不服氣別人的成績，於是拒絕承認自身不足、拒絕吸收他人經驗，從根本上喪失了學習的機會。耳朵關了，眼睛閉了，經驗進不來——關上它們的不是驕傲，是面子。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 You ask others "What indicator do you use?" but never "How did you figure that out?" Arrogant people think they don't need to learn, and they're not convinced by others' achievements, so they refuse to admit their own shortcomings and refuse to absorb others' experience—losing the chance to learn altogether. Ears shut, eyes closed, experience can't get in. And what shuts them isn't arrogance—it's ego.

qa.q: 放下自負、虛心學習，具體表現為什麼樣的行為？你今天能做的一件小事是什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 要你誇一句別人賺得多，你喉嚨裡那句「可是」先出來了——先出來的永遠是它。以實際盈虧而非嘴上成績論成敗；承認別人到手的真實利潤，不做想像中的勝利者——那句「可是」替你擋下的，不是輸贏，是面子。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 When you're asked to admit someone else made a lot, that "but" in your throat comes out first—it's always first. Success is judged by real profit and loss, not by words; acknowledge the real profit others have earned, don't be a victor in your imagination. That "but" doesn't shield you from losing—it shields your ego.

qa.q: 作者為什麼說「學習」這種常識本不該多講，卻又非講不可？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你也知道該學習，就像知道該早睡一樣。因為「活到老學到老」本是簡單常識，不該多講；但偏偏股票投資領域大部分人拒絕學習，所以有必要在此重申。常識要人提醒才記得，多半是因為照做就得承認自己過去幾年走錯了路。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 You know you should learn, just like you know you should sleep early. Because "live and learn" is simple common sense—it shouldn't need saying. But in the stock investment world, most people refuse to learn, so it's worth repeating. When common sense needs a reminder to be remembered, it's usually because following it would mean admitting you've taken the wrong path for years.

qa.q: 長線5倍 vs 短線10倍，作者用哪個標準論英雄？你平時用哪個標準？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 年底算總帳那件事，你已經拖了兩年。長線短線本身無優劣之分，關鍵在於到手的真實盈虧；想像中的10倍不如實際的5倍，投資成敗最終以真實盈虧為準。你拖著不算，怕的不是數字難看，是算出來的自己跟講出去的自己對不上。
keywords: 作者用哪個標準論英雄
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 That year-end settlement you've been putting off for two years? Long-term and short-term have no intrinsic superiority; what matters is the real profit you've got in hand. An imagined 10x isn't better than an actual 5x—investing success ultimately comes down to true gains and losses. You're not putting it off because the numbers are scary; it's because the person you'd calculate wouldn't match the person you've been presenting.

qa.q: 你以為技術指標能「指揮」股價嗎？作者說它對價格走勢到底有什麼用、沒什麼用？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你把三條均線調了又調，就為了等它給你一個買字。技術指標對價格走勢沒有任何指導意義，任何指標都不能操縱價格走勢；它只是專門用來跟蹤市場的工具。指望指標指揮行情，方向就錯了——你要的從來不是信號，是一個替你扛責任的人；怕的不是買錯，是沒人替你說「該買」。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 You kept adjusting those three moving averages, just waiting for one to tell you "buy." Technical indicators have zero predictive power over price movements; no indicator can control the market. They're only tools for tracking. To expect an indicator to steer the market is to look in the wrong direction—what you've never wanted was a signal; you wanted someone to blame. You're not afraid of buying wrong; you're afraid no one will say "buy" for you.

qa.q: 指標不能預測、不能操縱，那它到底好在哪裡？值得你天天看嗎？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你翻遍教程找「必漲指標」，其實是在找水晶球。它能非常有效地跟蹤價格走勢，向使用者揭示價格走勢的方向、空間、時間等重要信息，這是指標的意義所在。它是一面跟蹤的鏡子，不是一盞預測的水晶球——你非要它預測，是貪那份「提前知道」的安心。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 You've scoured every tutorial looking for a "sure-win indicator," but what you're really searching for is a crystal ball. What it can do is track price movements very effectively, revealing important info like direction, space, and timing to the user—that's what indicators are for. It's a mirror that tracks, not a crystal ball that predicts—if you insist it predicts, you're just clinging to that "knowing ahead of time" comfort.

qa.q: 指標告訴你方向、空間、時間之後，下一步該做什麼？作者怎麼串起這條鏈？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你常常是先買了，再找指標來解釋自己為什麼買。指標揭示價格走勢的方向、空間、時間等信息，指導使用者更合理地制定投資策略，使策略盡可能接近市場的真實走勢。先讀懂跟蹤信息，再製定策略——順序一顛倒，指標就從工具變成了藉口。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 Half the time, you buy first and then hunt for an indicator to explain why. Indicators reveal direction, space, timing, and other info about price movements, guiding users to build smarter investment strategies that stay as close as possible to the market's real moves. Read the tracking info first, then make your strategy—flip that order, and the indicator goes from being a tool to being an excuse.

qa.q: 走勢、指標、你——三者誰先誰後？把順序搞反會怎樣？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 指標走壞了，你卻說「這指標不準」——那一刻你把順序倒了過來。市場價格走勢在前面走，技術指標在後面跟蹤，然後投資人按照指標揭示的方向、空間、時間等制定合理投資策略並進行買賣操作。順序不可顛倒：是行情決定指標，不是指標決定行情。你倒過來，是因為承認走勢變了，就得承認自己買錯了。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 When the indicator breaks down, you say "this thing's useless"—and right then, you flipped the order. Market price moves first, technical indicators track from behind, and then investors use that direction, space, timing info to form a reasonable strategy and execute trades. The order can't be reversed: the market decides the indicator, not the other way around. You flip it because admitting the trend changed means admitting you bought wrong.

qa.q: 為什麼再神的指標也動不了股價一根汗毛？它的本質是什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你買指標買到上千塊，心裡卻隱隱相信它「比較準」。因為技術指標只是跟蹤市場價格走勢的工具，其本質是反映、跟蹤走勢而非影響走勢，所以對價格走勢沒有任何指導意義。你花的那筆錢，買的不是準確率，是那份「這下不會再錯了」的安慰。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 You spend a fortune on indicators, yet deep down you half-believe they're "more accurate." But technical indicators are just tools that track market price action—their essence is to reflect and follow trends, not influence them, so they have zero predictive power over price direction. That money you spent wasn't buying accuracy; it was buying the comfort of "at least this time I can't be wrong."

qa.q: 正確使用指標的順序是什麼？你現在的使用順序對嗎？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你常常是手指先動，策略後補。先明白指標是跟蹤市場的工具，再善用其跟蹤優勢，依指標揭示的走勢方向、空間、時間制定合理投資策略，最後進行買賣操作。這四步你跳過的中間兩步，不是不會，是忍不住——一分鐘都等不了。
keywords: 你現在的使用順序對嗎
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 Your fingers usually move first, and the strategy catches up later. First understand that indicators are tracking tools, then use their tracking advantage well, build a sensible investment strategy based on the direction, space, and timing they reveal, and finally make your trades. The middle two steps you skip? Not because you can't—it's because you can't stand waiting. Not even a minute.

qa.q: 指標能告訴你「漲還是跌」「漲到哪」「漲多久」嗎？它到底能給你什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你盯著指標，其實是在問它「還能拿嗎」。能獲得價格走勢的方向、空間、時間等重要信息，並以此為依據更合理地制定自己的投資策略。信息是給策略用的，不是給情緒用的——你那句「還能拿嗎」，問的從來不是策略，是怕。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 When you stare at the indicator, you're really asking it "can I still hold this?" It gives you key info on price direction, space, timing, and you can use that to shape a smarter strategy of your own. Info is meant for strategy, not for emotions—that "can I still hold?" you keep asking was never about strategy. It's about fear.

qa.q: 指標到底有沒有用？作者給出的答案為什麼是「既沒用又有用」？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你截圖發羣裡，多半是挑對了的那幾張。指標對價格走勢無指導意義，但最大優勢在於能有效跟蹤走勢、揭示關鍵信息，從而對投資人制定策略非常有用。用對地方就有用，用錯地方就無用——你用它來證明自己對的那一刻，它就已經沒用了，護的只是面子。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 When you screenshot and post it in the group, it's usually only the calls you got right. Indicators have no predictive power over price action, but their biggest strength is tracking trends effectively and revealing key info, which makes them super useful for building strategy. Use them right and they work; use them wrong and they're useless—the moment you use one to prove you were right, it's already done its job, and all you're protecting is your pride.

qa.q: 你的投資策略，依據的是指標揭示的信息，還是你昨天的感覺？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 問你「為什麼買這隻」，你答的是「感覺要起來了」。書裡的答案是：依據技術指標揭示的價格走勢方向、空間、時間等信息來制定，努力使自己的投資策略盡可能接近市場的真實走勢。「感覺」之所以好用，是因為它不用負責——說不出依據，就不用承認看錯。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 Ask you "why did you buy this one?" and you answer "it just feels like it's about to take off." The textbook answer: build your strategy based on the direction, space, and timing info the indicator reveals, and try your best to get it as close as possible to the market's real movement. "Feeling" is convenient because it never has to take responsibility—if you can't state your reasoning, you don't have to admit you got it wrong.

qa.q: 指標的「有用」體現在哪裡？它能替你做的和不能替你做的，分別是什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你想要的其實不是指標，是一句「買」。體現在它能非常有效地跟蹤價格走勢，向使用者揭示方向、空間、時間等信息，進而指導其制定更合理的投資策略。它能替你看清走勢，不能替你承擔決定——你要它替你承擔的那一刻，藏的是怕。
qa.a_en: Hey there! 😊 What you really want isn't an indicator—it's a "buy" signal. It's about tracking price movement effectively, revealing direction, space, time, and more to guide smarter investment decisions. It can help you see the trend clearly, but it can't make the call for you—the moment you want it to take that responsibility, what's hiding underneath is fear.

qa.q: 短線和長線，哪個更能賺錢？你被這個問題糾纏過多久？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 「到底做長線還是短線」這個問題，你問了三年。短線、長線其實都能賺錢，並無絕對優劣。問題在於何種情況下做長線、何種情況下做短線，須依市場趨勢靈活抉擇。你遲遲不決，不是選不出來，是怕選了就得負責；拖著，虧了還能說是方法沒定。
qa.a_en: Hey there! 😊 "Long-term or short-term?"—you've been asking this for three years. Both short-term and long-term can make money; there's no absolute right or wrong. The real question is when to go long and when to go short—it depends on market trends and requires flexible choices. You keep hesitating not because you can't decide, but because you're afraid that once you choose, you'll have to own it. Keep dragging it out, and if you lose, you can still say the method was never settled.

qa.q: 幾天算短線、幾個月算長線？這個界線作者怎麼畫？你怎麼畫？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你拿「打算拿一個月」來決定持股多久，行情可沒答應。短線長線難以界定，作者主張用趨勢決定投資週期：大趨勢向上時長期持有，大趨勢向下時做短線差價，這是最合理也最實用的方法。你愛用日曆，是因為日子到了就可以賣，不必承認是看錯了。
qa.a_en: Hey there! 😊 You're using "I plan to hold for a month" to decide your holding period—but the market never agreed to that. Short-term vs. long-term is hard to define; the author suggests letting the trend decide your investing cycle: hold long when the big trend points up, trade short-term swings when it points down. That's the most rational and practical approach. You love the calendar because when the date arrives, you can just sell—without having to admit you were wrong.

qa.q: 大勢向下時，你卻說「反正長期投資」——作者會怎麼說你？為什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 跌了三成，你對自己說「長期投資，不看盤了」。空頭走勢中應以短線差價為主，見好就收。因為大勢向下若做長線只會浪費金錢、消耗本金，短線快進快出才能保住已得利潤與本金。你那句「長期投資」，說出口的時候其實是不甘——不忍心認賠，就換個好聽的名字。
qa.a_en: Hey there! 😊 Down 30%, and you tell yourself, "Long-term investing, I'm not watching the charts." In a bear market, you should focus on short-term trading, locking in gains while you can. Because when the overall trend is down, going long just wastes money and drains your capital—quick in and out is how you protect both your profits and your principal. That "long-term investing" line? The moment you said it, it was really about not being willing to accept the loss—so you gave it a prettier name.

qa.q: 大勢向上時，你卻天天高拋低吸做差價——作者會怎麼說你？為什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 漲勢裡你一天進出兩趟，年底一算只賺了手續費。多頭走勢中應順應趨勢長期持有，輕易不要做短線差價。因為大勢向上，頻繁做短線會浪費行情、損失利益，長線持有才能充分享受上漲行情。你拿不住，不是不會，是手癢——每天不按兩下，就覺得這天白過了。
qa.a_en: Hey there! 😊 In an uptrend, you're in and out twice a day, and at year-end you find you only made enough to cover the fees. In a bull market, you should follow the trend and hold long-term—don't casually trade short-term swings. Because when the big picture is up, frequent short-term trading wastes the move and sacrifices gains; holding long-term is how you truly ride the rally. You can't hold—not because you don't know how, but because your hands get itchy. If you don't click buy/sell a couple times a day, it feels like the day went to waste.

qa.q: 「浪費金錢」和「浪費行情」，你更常犯哪一種？兩者分別錯在哪？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 跌的時候你拿著，漲的時候你跑了——一年下來兩頭空。空頭市場股價趨勢向下，長期持股只會繼續虧損、消耗本金；多頭市場趨勢向上，頻繁做短線容易錯過主升行情，白白浪費行情與利益。方向與週期不匹配，就是雙向浪費；而讓你兩頭都站錯的，是同一個怕。
qa.a_en: Hey there! 😊 When it drops, you hold; when it rises, you run—end of the year, you've got nothing on both ends. In a bear market, holding long-term just keeps losing and draining your capital; in a bull market, frequent short-term trading makes you miss the main rally, wasting the move and the money. When direction and timeframe don't match, it's a double waste—and the thing that has you standing on the wrong side both times is the same fear.

qa.q: 為什麼「趨勢」能一句話解決「短線還是長線」的千年之爭？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你還在羣裡爭「長線好還是短線好」，盤面早就給過答案。短線長線本無明確界限，而趨勢決定股價走向：順勢而為，上升趨勢持有、下降趨勢快進快出，方法簡單實用，符合化繁為簡、安全賺錢的理念。爭論比服從容易，因為服從趨勢等於承認自己之前站錯邊。
qa.a_en: Hey there! 😊 You're still arguing in the group about "long-term vs. short-term," but the charts have already answered. There's no clear line between short and long anyway—trend decides where price goes: follow it, hold when it's rising, get in and out fast when it's falling. Simple, practical, and aligned with keeping things simple and making money safely. Arguing is easier than obeying, because obeying the trend means admitting you've been on the wrong side all along.

qa.q: 「化繁為簡」在這一章具體化成了什麼？你的操作複雜到哪一步了？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你的交易規則寫了八條，沒有一條能在開盤那分鐘用得上。體現順勢而為、化繁為簡的理念：不糾結短線長線之爭，而以趨勢為唯一行為準則，先界定多空再選擇持股週期，做到安全、有效地賺錢。規則寫得越複雜，越好在虧的時候找藉口——哪一條都能怪，就怪不到自己。
qa.a_en: Hey there! 😊 Your trading rules have eight points, and not a single one can be applied in that first minute after the open. It's about going with the trend and simplifying: no more agonizing over short vs. long—trend is the only rule. Define bull or bear first, then choose your holding cycle, so you can make money safely and effectively. The more complex your rules, the easier it is to find an excuse when you lose—you can blame any of them, just never yourself.

qa.q: 空頭做長線、多頭做短線，兩種「搞反」的下場分別是什麼？你中過哪一個？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你可能兩種都犯過：跌的時候死抱，漲的時候急跑。空頭市場做長線是浪費金錢、消耗本金，多頭市場做短線是浪費行情、損失利益。週期選擇必須與大趨勢一致，方向搞反必然造成損失——奇怪的是你兩次都不是算錯的，是不甘：一次不甘認賠，一次不甘少賺。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 You've probably done both: holding tight when it's falling, and running off when it's rising. Going long in a bear market is just burning money and draining your capital; trading short-term in a bull market is wasting the trend and throwing away profits. Your cycle choice has to match the big trend—getting the direction wrong will always cost you. The funny thing is, neither time was about bad math—it was about not wanting to let go: once you couldn't accept the loss, once you couldn't accept making less.

qa.q: 「見好就收」四個字，作者是在什麼市場裡教你的？你用得出來嗎？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 跌勢裡難得賺了兩個點，你卻想再等等，等它多走一根。見好就收指短線操作獲利後及時了結、不貪多，適用於大趨勢向下的空頭市場：以短線差價為主，快進快出，保住已獲利潤。那句「再等等」說起來像耐心，其實就是貪。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 You finally made two points in a downtrend, and instead of taking it, you want to wait, let it run one more candle. Taking profits while they're good means closing out after a short-term win without getting greedy—it works in a bear market where the big trend is down: focus on short-term spreads, get in and out fast, and protect what you've already made. That 'wait a little longer' sounds like patience, but it's really just greed.

qa.q: 作者反覆強調的週期選擇關鍵，用一句話總結是什麼？你記得住、做得到嗎？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 買入前那兩句話你背得出，下單時卻從來沒問過。服從趨勢、區分多空：大趨勢向下宜做短線差價，大趨勢向上宜長期持有，切不可顛倒，否則不是浪費金錢就是浪費行情。你跳過這兩問，是怕答案跟你想買的那隻對不上。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 You know those two questions by heart before you buy, but somehow you never ask them when you place the order. Follow the trend and know your market: when the big trend is down, play short-term spreads; when it's up, hold long-term. Never flip them, or you'll either burn money or waste the rally. You skip those two questions because you're afraid the answers won't match the stock you want to buy.

qa.q: 「買在最低、賣在最高」——這個願望你也有過吧？作者說它是什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 賣掉之後它又漲了兩根，你盯著螢幕算了三天那筆「少賺的」。書裡主張放棄「最低價買入、最高價賣出」的幻想，因為這是很幼稚的想法、很天真的願望，理智的投機者不應對此抱有任何幻想。你算的不是那兩根，是不甘。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 After you sold, it ticked up two more candles, and you spent three days staring at the screen calculating that 'lost profit.' The book says to let go of the fantasy of 'buying at the lowest and selling at the highest'—it calls it a childish notion, a naïve wish that no rational speculator should entertain. What you're calculating isn't the two candles—it's the unwillingness to accept it.

qa.q: 為什麼你永遠無法製造一個「最低價」或「最高價」？這件事由誰說了算？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你把買價設在分時圖那根最低針上，然後等了兩個月。因為人根本沒有辦法製造一個最低價或最高價，極端價位無法被預測或被創造，這是不得不接受的現實。價格由眾人的集體行為決定，不由你的願望決定。你等的不是價位，是怕自己一買就跌，所以乾脆永遠不買。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 You set your buy price right at that lowest wick on the intraday chart, and then waited two months. The thing is, nobody can create a lowest or highest price—extreme levels can't be predicted or manufactured, and that's just reality you have to accept. Prices are driven by the collective actions of everyone, not by your wish. What you're waiting for isn't a price point—it's the fear that you'll buy and it'll drop, so you'd rather never buy at all.

qa.q: 連能操控股價的莊家都做不到極端價位進出——你憑什麼覺得自己可以？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你想在最低點接貨，就得有人在那個點上不顧一切地割。股票交易不是一個人玩的遊戲，沒人會像傻瓜一樣在價位不再下跌時爭先賣出籌碼，多數人也不會在同一天集體失去理智去配合你。市場不是為你一個人設的——你把希望押在別人犯傻上，圖的是那份「我抄到底了」的優越，其實是僥倖。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 For you to catch the absolute bottom, someone has to be panic-selling right at that point. Trading isn't a one-person game—nobody's going to play the fool and scramble to dump their shares once the price has stopped falling, and most people aren't going to collectively lose their minds on the same day just to line up with your timing. The market isn't built around you—you're betting on others being stupid, chasing that little thrill of thinking, 'I caught the bottom.' That's not insight—that's just luck.

qa.q: 莊家資金那麼大，為什麼反而更做不到「最低買、最高賣」？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你羨慕莊家資金大，卻沒想過他根本跑不掉。機構資金所需要的籌碼不是一手或兩手，而是巨量，根本不可能在單一極端價位全部買進或賣出。越大越靈活不了，這正是市場的公平之處。你手裡那幾手隨時能走，卻偏要學人家重倉，貪的是人家的氣派，丟的是自己的優勢。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 You envy the big players for their huge capital, but you never stop to think—they can't get out. Institutional money doesn't trade in one or two lots; it's massive, so there's no way they can buy or sell everything at a single extreme price. The bigger you are, the less flexible you become—and that's what keeps the market fair. Your few lots can bail anytime, but you'd rather mimic heavy positioning. You covet their swagger while throwing away your own edge.

qa.q: 作者把「總想買最低賣最高」比作什麼？你聽完還笑得出來嗎？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你每天早上準時開軟體，像是去老地方看看有沒有人掉了錢包。書裡把總想在最低價買入、最高價賣出的人，比作總是希望每天都能在同一個地方撿到巨額資金或價值連城寶藏一樣可笑。天天做同一個夢，夢裡不會有真金。你天天去，不是因為機會在那兒，是因為不去就得承認沒機會。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 Every morning you're on time to open the software, like checking your favorite spot to see if someone dropped a wallet. The book compares people who always want to buy at the lowest and sell at the highest to folks who keep hoping to stumble upon a fortune or priceless treasure in the same spot every single day—it's just laughable. Dreaming the same dream every day won't produce real gold. You show up daily, not because opportunity lives there, but because not showing up means admitting there's no opportunity at all.

qa.q: 讓市場裡大多數人同一天「集體犯傻」來成全你——這需要什麼條件？你有嗎？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你那筆「完美成交」，得讓幾萬個人在同一分鐘一起失去理智。一個人瘋了、失去理智有可能這樣做，但要大多數人在同一天都失去理智或發瘋，必須具備超人類的能力纔可，現實中不可能。你不是超人，市場也不會配合。你遲遲不下單，等的不是那個價，是怕一買就錯，所以把決定權推給一個不會出現的價位。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 That "perfect fill" you're waiting for? It would take tens of thousands of people all losing their minds at the exact same minute. One person going crazy and acting irrational? Possible. But most people all losing it on the same day? That takes superhuman abilities — not happening in reality. You're not Superman, and the market won't cooperate. The reason you keep hesitating to place that order isn't the price you're waiting for — it's that you're afraid of buying wrong. So you push the decision onto a price that will never show up.

qa.q: 連能控制高低價的人都做不到的事，你一個控制不了股價的人，憑什麼要求？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你能接受的賣點，是不是永遠比帳戶裡那條成本高？既然能夠控制低價、高價的人都無法實現最低價進去、最高價出來，那麼沒有控制能力的人，更沒有資格要求得到這樣的結果。要求超出能力，是幻想；接受現實，是成熟。你遲遲不肯成熟，是因為一成熟就得承認那筆虧是自己造成的。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 The sell point you can accept — is it always above that cost line in your account? If even the people who can control lows and highs can't buy at the absolute lowest and sell at the absolute highest, then someone with no control has no right to demand that kind of result. Demanding beyond your ability is fantasy. Accepting reality is maturity. The reason you keep putting off being mature? Because once you're mature, you have to admit that loss was your own doing.

qa.q: 作者最後給你的忠告就一句話——你猜是什麼？你聽得進去嗎？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你心裡那條線，是不是「跌到這裡就反彈、再到那裡我就走」？書末的忠告只有一句：放棄可笑幻想；否則你就不是一個成功的投機者，或者說你實在不太適合投機這個行當。聽不進去也正常——幻想之所以難戒，是它從來不要求你當場承認自己錯了。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 That line in your head — is it "if it drops to here it'll bounce, and when it gets there I'll leave"? The only advice at the end of the book is this: drop the ridiculous fantasy. Otherwise, you're not a successful speculator — or frankly, you're just not cut out for this game. It's normal if you can't take it in — fantasies are hard to quit because they never require you to admit you're wrong on the spot.

qa.q: 既然完美價位不可求，那買賣的目標應該設在哪裡？作者的方法論落點是什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你把價位填到小數點後兩位，然後一次都沒成交過。交易結果取決於市場眾人的集體行為而非個人意願，應接受不可預知的極端價位，轉而追求務實可實現的買賣區間。你寧可不成交也不肯將就，護的不是收益，是面子——萬一買貴了兩毛，就沒法跟人說自己買得漂亮。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 You fill in your price to two decimal places — and you've never gotten a single fill. Trading results depend on the collective behavior of the market, not your personal wishes. You should accept that extreme prices are unpredictable and instead aim for realistic, achievable buy and sell ranges. You'd rather not get filled than settle — what you're protecting isn't your profit, it's your pride. If you paid two cents more, you couldn't brag about how cleanly you bought.

qa.q: 買股票是為了賺錢，還是為了「跑贏別人」？你捫心自問，答案是哪個？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你手裡那隻這個月賺了八個點，你還是嫌它慢，因為隔壁那隻漲停了。書裡主張不必非要買漲得最快的那隻股票，只要手中股票能賺錢就好，不必考慮誰能獲得第一名，放棄與他人比較的心態。你嫌的不是它慢，是不甘——別人賺得比你多，比你自己賺到還刺眼。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 That stock you're holding made 8% this month, and you still think it's slow, because the one next to it hit the limit up. The book says you don't have to buy the fastest-rising stock — as long as the one you hold makes money, that's good enough. No need to compete for first place, and no need to compare with others. What you're complaining about isn't that it's slow — it's the sting of unfairness. Someone else making more than you hurts more than you making money yourself.

qa.q: 九成人都想買「漲得最快的」——作者說這錯在哪裡？錯在「最快」還是「買」？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你選股時先看的，是它今年漲了第幾名。其實投資目的是賺錢而非比賽爭第一。追求最快者永遠不滿足手中股票的漲升速度，嫉妒別人的股票漲得快，反而陷入追逐最快的誤區。錯在把比賽當成了目的——你看排名的那雙眼睛，看的不是行情，是不甘。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 When you pick stocks, the first thing you check is where it ranks in gains this year. But the point of investing is to make money, not to win a contest. People who chase the fastest are never satisfied with the speed of what they hold. They envy others' stocks for rising too fast, and end up trapped in the trap of chasing the quickest. The mistake is treating the race as the goal — those eyes of yours staring at the rankings aren't looking at the market, they're looking at resentment.

qa.q: 一心追「最快」的人，最後通常栽在哪裡？這條路是怎麼一步步走岔的？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你上個月換了四次股，每一次的理由都是「那隻看起來更好」。這會使人頻繁換股，陷入追逐最快的誤區，最終往往賺不到錢。因為總覺得別人的股票漲得快，無法安心持有——頻繁換股的盡頭，是頻繁虧損。你每次換股都在許願，許的是僥倖。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 You switched stocks four times last month, and every single time the reason was "that one looks better." This kind of behavior makes you switch constantly, falling into the trap of chasing the fastest — and in the end, usually no money is made. Because you always feel others' stocks are rising faster, so you can't hold anything with peace of mind. The end of frequent switching is frequent losses. Every time you switch stocks, you're making a wish — and the wish is luck.

qa.q: 醫院排隊換行、換來換去反而最慢——這個故事你聽懂了嗎？它說的是排隊，還是你？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你在銀行排隊，看旁邊那條動了一下就換過去——換完它就不動了。這說明頻繁換股就像排隊換行，換來換去反而總排在最後，眼看別人已到窗口。比喻手裡的股票換來換去，最後結果也不會好。你換隊那一下，不是算過，是忍不住。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 You're waiting in line at the bank, and the moment the line next to you moves, you switch over — and then it stops moving. That's what frequent switching is like: jumping from line to line, only to end up at the back again while others reach the window. It's a metaphor — switch your stocks around all you want, the result won't be any better. That move you made wasn't calculated. You just couldn't help yourself.

qa.q: 作者對「股票投資的目的」給出的答案是什麼？你認同嗎？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 年底曬收益的時候，你最在意的是自己排第幾。書裡把目的界定為賺錢而非比賽。投資不是為了獲得第一名，只要賺錢就好，不應以漲速排名來衡量成敗。你要那個名次，要的不是錢，是面子。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 At year-end when everyone's showing off their returns, what you care most about is where you rank. The book defines the purpose as making money, not a race. Investing isn't about being first; as long as you make money, that's good. You shouldn't judge success by ranking based on speed of gains. That ranking you want—it's not money you're after, it's face.

qa.q: 「要比別人漲得快」的人，為什麼反而賺不到錢？他的錢被什麼喫掉了？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你賣掉的那隻，後來漲了三成；你換去的那隻，套到現在。這種人一直不滿足手頭股票的漲升速度，總嫉妒沒持有的股票漲得更快，於是頻繁換股，結果如同排隊換行，始終落於人後。錢被「比較」喫掉了——比較這件事不花錢，卻最貴，因為它從不讓你承認是自己換錯了。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 The one you sold later went up 30%; the one you switched to is still stuck. This kind of person is never satisfied with how fast their own stocks are rising, and always jealous that stocks they don't own are climbing faster. So they switch frequently, and the result is like switching lines in a queue—they end up always behind. Your money gets eaten up by 'comparison.' Comparison itself is free, but it's the most expensive thing, because it never lets you admit that you made the wrong switch.

qa.q: 作者要求你對自己手中的股票有什麼心態？你現在有嗎？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你手裡那隻慢慢漲，你卻天天刷別人的漲停。書裡要求知足與專注：只要自己的股票在賺錢就應滿足，不必眼紅別人的漲速，安心持有、不隨意換股，纔是正確理念。你眼紅的不是漲幅，是受不了別人比你風光——那點不甘，正在替你看盤。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 Your stock is climbing slowly, but you keep scrolling through other people's limit-up moves every day. The book calls for contentment and focus: as long as your own stock is making money, be satisfied. No need to envy others' speed. Hold them calmly and don't switch on a whim—that's the right approach. What you're jealous of isn't the gains. You just can't stand others having a better time than you—and that little resentment is the one actually watching your portfolio.

qa.q: 怎麼判斷自己是不是「換來換去」成癮了？怎麼戒？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你一天不自選股裡加兩隻新的就渾身不對勁。這表現為頻繁換股、追逐熱門與漲速最快的股票。避免之道是明確賺錢即目的的目標，對手中能獲利的股票保持信心與耐心。你那隻手停不下來，不是因為機會多，是手癢。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 If you don't add two new stocks to your watchlist in a day, you feel uneasy. It shows up as frequent switching, chasing hot stocks and the fastest movers. The way to avoid it is to be clear that making money is the goal, and to have confidence and patience in the stocks that are already profitable for you. That hand of yours can't stop—not because there are too many opportunities, but because it's itchy.

qa.q: 「簡單操作、安全賺錢」——八個字裡，你過去更看重哪四個？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你下單那天算的是「漲到多少我就賺多少」，沒算過反過來那一格。書裡主張「簡單操作，安全賺錢」，並強調安全賺錢是投資者必須具備的投資理念。股票投資風險大，買入即須承擔交易成本，故先求安全再求獲利。你跳過那一格，不是忘了，是怕——算了就不敢買了。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 The day you placed your order, you calculated, 'If it rises to this point, I'll make this much.' You never calculated the other direction. The book advocates 'simple operations, safe profit,' and stresses that safe profit is an investment philosophy every investor must have. Stock investing is risky. Once you buy, you have to take on trading costs. So safety comes first, then profit. You skipped that part—not because you forgot, but because you were scared. If you'd done the math, you'd never have bought.

qa.q: 買入那一刻，你的帳戶就已經虧了——你知道虧在哪裡嗎？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你按下買入的那秒鐘，帳戶已經先少了一筆。交易手續費、印花稅等固定成本是必須支付的，且市場中所有交易成本都由輸家承擔，買入後無論盈虧，這筆成本已先行付出。你從來不看那一欄，因為看了就得承認：有些交易，還沒開始就已經虧了。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 The second you pressed buy, your account already lost a bit. Fixed costs like commissions and stamp duty are unavoidable. And in this market, all trading costs are borne by the losers. After buying, win or lose, that cost is already paid. You never look at that line item, because if you did, you'd have to admit: some trades are already losing before they even start.

qa.q: 同樣一筆成本，贏家和輸家承受的為什麼不一樣？輸家到底多輸了什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 同樣一張單，贏的人少賺一點，輸的人卻多賠一份。贏家扣除交易成本只是利潤減少；輸家除扣除交易成本外還要承受差價損失，其中一部分差價損失正是替對方承擔交易成本的費用，雙重受損。你虧的那筆裡有一半是替對手付的——知道這件事還不停手，靠的是僥倖。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 On the same trade, the winner makes a little less, but the loser loses a little more. For the winner, deducting trading costs just reduces profits. For the loser, besides trading costs, there's also the spread loss—part of which is basically paying the other side's trading costs. Double damage. Half of what you lost was paying for your opponent. If you know that and still don't stop, you're relying on luck.

qa.q: 風險來臨的那一刻，你的第一個動作是什麼？作者說應該是什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 帳戶綠了那天，你第一件事是加倉，不是減倉。書裡說第一件事是保住本金，因為只有保住本金纔有賺錢的機會；一旦本金損失殆盡，即使機會來臨，也沒有資金去抓住機會。你加的那一筆，不是策略，是不甘——不甘心就這麼認輸。
keywords: 你的第一個動作是什麼
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 The day your account was down, the first thing you did was add to your position, not cut it. The book says the first thing is to protect your principal, because only by protecting your principal do you have a chance to make money. Once it's gone, even if an opportunity comes, you won't have any capital to grab it. That addition you made wasn't strategy—it was stubbornness. You just couldn't bear to admit defeat.

qa.q: 為什麼你的第一課不是「怎麼賺錢」，而是「怎麼止損」？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你買過的課程都叫「戰法」，沒有一門叫「怎麼認輸」。學會止損是安全賺錢的前提，不會止損就無法控制虧損、保住本金，安全賺錢也就無從談起，所以止損被列為投資的第一課。你繞開它，是因為認輸太傷面子，寧可再學一招。
keywords: 為什麼你的第一課不是
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 Every course you've bought is called a "battle tactic"—none of them is called "how to admit defeat." Learning to stop loss is the foundation of making money safely; without it, you can't control losses or protect your capital, so safe profits are out of the question. That's why stop loss is listed as the first lesson in investing. You avoid it because admitting defeat hurts your pride too much—you'd rather learn another trick.

qa.q: 「安全」和「賺錢」，作者把它們放在一起，誰在前面？為什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你把「這波能賺多少」寫在本子第一頁。安全賺錢強調先控風險、後求利潤：風險出現時先保住本金，透過止損避免大虧，是貫穿全書的核心投資理念，也是操作的總原則。你把順序記反了那麼多年，不是不懂，是貪。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 You wrote "how much can I make from this wave" on the first page of your notebook. Safe profit-making emphasizes controlling risk first, then seeking profit: when risk appears, protect your capital first, and avoid big losses through stop loss. That's the core investment philosophy running through the whole book, and the overall principle of operation. You've had the order backwards for years—not because you don't understand, but because you're greedy.

qa.q: 輸家為什麼是「雙重受損」？這種不公平你感受到過嗎？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你以為虧的就是帳面上那個數。其實輸家既要支付固定交易成本，又要承擔差價損失，成本與損失疊加，無形之中加劇了虧損的幅度，比贏家承受更大的雙重負擔。你知道了還不肯走，多半是在安慰自己「再等等就回來了」。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 You think the loss is just that number on your screen. But losers actually pay both fixed transaction costs and bear spread losses—costs and losses stack up, silently amplifying the damage, making them carry a heavier double burden than winners. You know this and still won't leave. Most likely you're telling yourself, "If I wait a little longer, it'll come back."

qa.q: 本金沒了，機會來了你能幹什麼？作者用一句話說清了這個關係，你能複述嗎？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 真正的機會來那天，你手上還有籌碼嗎？本金是參與市場、把握機會的資本，只有保住本金才能在機會來臨時有資金進場；本金耗盡，連入場資格都喪失，賺錢無從談起。你現在不肯止血，賭的不是行情回來，是僥倖。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 When the real opportunity comes, will you still have chips in hand? Capital is what lets you participate in the market and seize opportunities—only by protecting your capital can you have funds to enter when opportunity knocks. Run out of capital, and you lose your right to enter at all, so making money becomes impossible. You refuse to stop the bleeding now—you're not betting on the market coming back, you're betting on luck.

qa.q: 本章結尾說「後面將專門交待」的是什麼？你準備好了嗎？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 讀到這裡你點了頭，但「我不會止損」這句話還沒說出口。作者指出後面將專門就止損問題作詳細交待，本章以「止損是安全賺錢前提」點題，是止損策略教學的開篇理念鋪墊。承認不會，比學會更難——難的是面子。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 You nodded when you read this, but those words "I don't know how to stop loss" still haven't left your mouth. The author points out that he'll explain stop loss in detail later; this chapter uses "stop loss is the prerequisite for safe profit" as the theme, laying the conceptual groundwork for the stop-loss strategy lessons. Admitting you don't know is harder than learning—what's hard is face.

qa.q: 股價走勢到底有幾種？你能一口氣說全嗎？說不全的話，是你笨還是它複雜？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你電腦上開著七個視窗、十二條均線，卻說不清它在漲還是在跌。書裡主張股價走勢非常簡單，不是上漲就是下跌，走得藝術一點也就是橫盤整理，合計僅三種走勢，絕對不會有第四種走勢出現。它不複雜，複雜的是人——你把畫面搞得那麼複雜，是怕一簡化就沒藉口了。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 You've got seven windows and twelve moving averages open on your screen, but you can't even say whether it's going up or down. The book says stock price movements are very simple—either rising or falling, or if it wants to get artistic, it's just a sideways consolidation. That's only three possible moves, and there's absolutely no fourth. It's not complicated—what's complicated is people. You make your charts so messy because you're afraid that once you simplify, you'll lose your excuse.

qa.q: 走勢只有三種，賺錢是不是就該很簡單？簡單到什麼程度？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 這三句話你背得出，昨天卻一句都沒做到。上漲時買入，下跌時賣出，橫盤整理、看不清楚方向時就退出來觀望——如此簡單的操作，賺錢理應是一件非常容易的事情。你做不到，是因為第三句最難：退出來，就得承認自己看不清。
keywords: 賺錢是不是就該很簡單
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 You can recite those three sentences by heart, but yesterday you didn't follow through on a single one. Buy when it's rising, sell when it's falling, and when it's moving sideways and you can't see a clear direction, step back and wait—with such simple operations, making money should be a very easy thing. You can't do it because the third sentence is the hardest: stepping back means admitting you can't see clearly.

qa.q: 一本講股票的書，為什麼大半篇幅在講人？作者覺得問題出在誰身上？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你書架上十七本炒股書，沒有一本是講你自己的。因為股票價格走勢很簡單，基本上不需要太多的研究；問題在於投資股票的人太複雜了，所以要研究的重點是人而不是股票。你寧可再買一本書，也不肯回頭看自己的成交單——那上面寫滿了你不願承認的東西。
keywords: 為什麼大半篇幅在講人
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 You've got seventeen stock trading books on your shelf, but not one of them is about yourself. Because stock price movements are simple—they basically don't need much research. The problem is that the people investing in stocks are too complicated, so the focus of research should be on people, not stocks. You'd rather buy another book than look back at your own trade records—those are filled with things you don't want to admit.

qa.q: 該買的時候，你腦子裡轉的是哪句話？那句話最後害你錯過了什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你看好的那隻，從八塊看到十四塊，一股沒買。買入時總會想「現在買進高不高、買進以後套住了怎麼辦」，一直猶猶豫豫、遲遲不能下手，終於錯失了最佳的買入機會。你猶豫的不是價位，是怕——怕買了就跌，那就不只是虧錢，還得承認自己看錯。
keywords: 你腦子裡轉的是哪句話
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 That stock you liked—you watched it go from eight to fourteen and didn't buy a single share. Every time you're about to buy, you think, "Is it too high to buy now? What if I get stuck after buying?" You hesitate and hesitate, can't pull the trigger, and end up missing the best entry. What you're hesitating about isn't the price—it's fear. Fear that it'll drop right after you buy, and then it's not just losing money, you also have to admit you were wrong.

qa.q: 該賣的時候，你又在等什麼？「再漲一點」這四個字，你對自己說過多少次？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 該走的時候你說「再漲一點」，那一點永遠等不到。總是不捨得賣出，擔憂賣出之後繼續上漲怎麼辦，結果錯失了最佳的賣出機會；買賣兩端皆因患得患失而誤事。你那句「再漲一點」，說出口的是貪，不是判斷。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 When it's time to leave, you say, "Just a little more." But that little more never comes. You can't bear to sell, worried about missing further gains, and you blow the best exit. Both buying and selling get messed up because you're too busy worrying about what might go wrong. That "just a little more" you keep saying—that's greed talking, not judgment.

qa.q: 錯失良機是你的專利嗎？作者說它是什麼級別的毛病？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 聽到「大家都這樣」，你心裡那塊石頭是不是落了地？書裡認為這不是某一個投資人的弊端，幾乎是投資大眾的通病，人人都可能犯，值得所有投資者引以為戒。你鬆的那口氣，就是安慰——安慰一來，改變就不用開始了。
keywords: 錯失良機是你的專利嗎
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 When you hear "everyone's doing it," doesn't that stone in your heart just drop? The book says this isn't one investor's flaw—it's almost a common disease among the investing public. Anyone can fall for it, and every investor should take it as a warning. That sigh of relief you let out? That's comfort—and once comfort kicks in, change never starts.

qa.q: 既然複雜的是人，那要改的對象是誰？從哪裡下手？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 走勢就那幾條線，複雜的是你按下買入鍵的那隻手。所以該研究的對象不是市場，是你自己——花力氣研究自己，努力使自己的投資行為更趨向於簡單，以至於行為更接近市場走勢的客觀存在。只是大多數人寧願再去學一套新指標，也不肯承認要改的是自己。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 The price action is just a few lines. What's complicated is the hand that presses the buy button. So the thing you should study isn't the market—it's yourself. Put your energy into studying yourself, making your investing behavior simpler, until it aligns closer with the objective reality of the market's moves. But most people would rather learn yet another new indicator than admit the thing that needs changing is themselves.

qa.q: 「行為貼近走勢的客觀存在」——這句繞口的話，落到操作上是什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你每次下單前都要加一句「我覺得」——其實書裡說的簡單，即少摻雜主觀猶豫與情緒，按走勢簡單的客觀規律行事——漲則買、跌則賣、橫盤則觀望，行為與走勢保持一致。你那句「我覺得」不肯刪，是因為刪了就得承認：判斷錯了就是錯了，沒有「我覺得」可以躲。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 Before every order, you add, "I think." But what the book says is simple: cut out the subjective hesitation and emotion, follow the objective rules of the trend—buy when it rises, sell when it falls, wait when it's range-bound. Keep your behavior in sync with the trend. The reason you won't delete that "I think" is because once you do, you have to admit: a wrong call is a wrong call, and there's nowhere to hide behind "I think."

qa.q: 用一句話總結本章：賺錢難在哪裡？你認同這個答案嗎？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你一直以為是自己學得還不夠多。其實答案是化繁為簡：股價走勢本身很簡單，賺錢難在人性複雜；研究自己、簡化投資行為，纔是安全賺錢的根本之道。要你少學一點，比多學還難——少學就沒藉口了。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 You've always thought you just haven't learned enough. But the real answer is simplifying: price trends themselves are simple; the hard part is human nature. Studying yourself and simplifying your investing behavior is the fundamental way to make money safely. Telling you to learn less is harder than telling you to learn more—because if you learn less, you've got no excuses left.

qa.q: 你買股票前，先看的是大盤還是個股？作者說正確的順序是什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你打開軟體就直接搜自己的持股，大盤那頁從來不點。書裡主張「先看大盤、再看個股」的嚴謹態度，反對重個股、輕大盤；看不清大盤走勢時應退出觀望，不操作也是一種投資策略。你跳過大盤，是怕——看了就得承認現在不該買。
keywords: 先看的是大盤還是個股
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 You open the app and go straight to search your holdings. You never click on the market page. The book advocates a rigorous approach: "check the market first, then individual stocks," and warns against overemphasizing stocks while neglecting the broader market. When the market's direction is unclear, step back and wait—not trading is also an investment strategy. You skip the market because you're afraid—if you looked, you'd have to admit now isn't the time to buy.

qa.q: 大盤向下時，你的個股真的能「獨善其身」嗎？作者怎麼算這筆帳？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 大盤連跌五天，你還在翻自選股找「抗跌的」。大盤走勢向下時個股難以獨立向上，投資成功概率低；當收益與風險不成比例、風險大於收益時，應建議投資人出局而非繼續買進個股。你那段時間特別勤奮，勤奮裡藏的是不甘——不甘心空著手。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 The market's dropped five days in a row, and you're still scrolling through your watchlist looking for something "resilient." When the market trend is downward, individual stocks can hardly move up on their own—your odds of success are low. When the risk-reward ratio is out of whack and risk outweighs reward, investors should be advised to get out rather than keep buying. You were especially diligent during that time, but what hid in that diligence was unwillingness—unwilling to sit on your hands.

qa.q: 專家為什麼愛說「重個股、輕大盤」？他們在什麼情況下說這句話最「安全」？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 電視上那位老師最愛說「重個股、輕大盤」，漲跌他都贏。兩種情況：一是看不清大盤走勢時這樣說可以左右逢源，漲跌都對；二是趨勢向下時這樣說顯得自己更高一籌，同樣達到漲跌都對的效果。說這句話，是為了讓自己永遠不錯。你愛聽，是因為聽了虧了也不用承認是自己選錯。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 That teacher on TV loves saying "focus on the stock, not the market index." He wins either way, up or down. Two scenarios: one, when the market trend isn't clear, saying this lets him play both sides—right whether it goes up or down; two, when the trend is downward, saying this makes him look sharper, again covering both outcomes. He says it to make sure he's never wrong. You love hearing it because when you lose money, you don't have to admit you picked wrong.

qa.q: 「重個股、輕大盤」聽起來像投資策略，作者說它其實是什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你在羣裡分析得頭頭是道，回頭自己的倉卻是虧的。它是說股的一種方法，目的是為了盡可能地說對、讓話語漲跌都對；而投資者是用真金白銀買賣股票，目的是賺錢，本質完全不同。你越講越起勁，是因為講對了有面子，買對了可不一定。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 You analyze everything so impressively in the group, but your own positions end up losing. That's the way of a stock talker—its goal is to be as right as possible, to make words work whether the market rises or falls. But investors buy and sell stocks with real money, aiming to make profits—completely different in nature. The more you talk, the more excited you get, because being right earns you face. But buying right? Not necessarily.

qa.q: 看不清時，動手和不動手，哪個更虧？作者幫你算過這筆帳嗎？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 空倉那幾天你坐立難安，好像不買就白開了戶。算筆帳：不介入最大的損失就是不賺錢；介入則結果有可能賺錢也有可能虧損。當投資收益與風險不成比例時，不介入比冒險介入更明智。帳你會算，手卻不聽——那是手癢，不是判斷。
keywords: 作者幫你算過這筆帳嗎
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 Those days you stayed in cash, you were restless, like not buying meant your account was pointless. Let's do the math: the biggest loss from not getting in is simply not making money. But if you get in, you could make money or lose money. When the return doesn't justify the risk, staying out is smarter than diving in. You know how to calculate, but your hands won't listen—that's itchy fingers, not judgment.

qa.q: 說股的人和你，目的有什麼不同？為什麼他的「金句」不能當你的操作？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你轉發的那句「別人恐懼時我貪婪」，自己也沒照做過。說股者與投資者的目的不一樣：說股是為向人解釋股票為何漲跌、力求說對；投資是為賺錢。目的不同，所以適合說股的理念不能作為投資策略。你收藏的不是依據，是講起來體面的面子。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 You shared that quote, "Be greedy when others are fearful," but you never followed it yourself. Stock talkers and investors have different goals: talking aims to explain why stocks rise and fall, to be as "right" as possible; investing aims to make money. Different goals mean a philosophy suited for talking can't be your investment strategy. What you saved isn't a principle—it's face you can show off.

qa.q: 看不清方向時，你通常會怎麼做？作者建議你怎麼做？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 「我看不清」這四個字，你多久沒說過了？建議退出觀望、不操作，因為不介入最大損失只是不賺錢；等看清形勢再行動，避免在風險大於收益的環境下貿然買進。說不出這四個字，是因為一說就得承認自己不懂——而不動手，等於承認自己多餘。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 "I can't see clearly"—how long has it been since you said those four words? My advice: step back, watch, and don't trade. Because the biggest loss from not getting in is just not making money; wait until the picture clears before acting, and avoid jumping in when risk outweighs reward. You can't say those words because saying them means admitting you don't know—and not acting means admitting you're unnecessary.

qa.q: 投資者和說股者，誰需要為自己的話負責？你平時更像哪一個？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你跟朋友講「我看好這隻」，自己一股沒買。投資者必須先看大盤再看個股，用嚴謹態度對待真金白銀的買賣；說股者只需讓話語漲跌都對，不必對實際盈虧負責，兩者不可混同。你講的時候不用負責，所以講得特別順——那份順暢，蓋住的是你不敢下注的怕。
keywords: 誰需要為自己的話負責
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 You told a friend, "I like this stock," but you didn't buy a single share yourself. An investor must look at the market first, then the stock, treating real-money trades with discipline. A stock talker only needs words that work in both directions, with no responsibility for real gains or losses—these two can't be mixed. You speak without responsibility, so it flows smoothly—but that smoothness is just covering the fear of not daring to bet.

qa.q: 把「先大盤後個股」變成動作，第一步是什麼？你明天能做嗎？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 明天開盤前，試著先看一眼大盤。以大盤方向為先決判斷：大盤向下、看不清時就不進場，退出觀望等待機會；形勢明朗後再依大盤定個股操作的時機與倉位。這一步你一直跳過，不是不會，是怕看了就得放下那隻想買的。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 Before the market opens tomorrow, try looking at the index first. Use the market direction as your primary call: if it's falling or unclear, stay out, sit on the sidelines, and wait for a chance; once the picture is clear, use the market to decide your timing and position in individual stocks. You've always skipped this step—not because you can't, but because you're afraid that once you look, you'll have to let go of the stock you want to buy.

qa.q: 你平時盯的是「個股」還是「市場」？本書說你真正活在什麼裡面？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你一開盤就直奔自己的持倉，大盤漲跌懶得掃一眼。主張用十分的精力瞭解市場。因為投資者是在市場裡生存，不是在某一隻股票裡生存，不瞭解市場就無法在市場中生存，所以瞭解市場遠比了解個股重要。你只盯自己那隻，是怕看大盤會澆冷水；可躲開潮水，浪打來時你連逃的方向都沒有。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 The moment the market opens, you rush straight to your holdings without even glancing at the index. The advice is to put full effort into understanding the market. Because investors survive in the market, not in a single stock—if you don't understand the market, you can't survive in it, so understanding the market matters far more than understanding any one stock. You only stare at your own stock because you're afraid the market view will pour cold water on you. But if you hide from the tide, when the wave hits, you won't even know which way to run.

qa.q: 你也覺得「我只研究我的股票就夠了」嗎？本書怎麼反駁這句話？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你鑽研一隻股票鑽到半夜，從不抬頭看整片海。有人認為投資股票不是開設股票市場，瞭解市場意義不大甚至完全沒必要。本章斥之為無知的見解，強調投資股票之前必須知道自己是在市場裡生存，不瞭解市場怎麼能在市場裡生存。你躲進個股，是怕「退潮」那句話澆醒自己；不肯問漲退，因為答案可能你不愛聽。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 You dig into one single stock till the middle of the night, never once lifting your head to see the whole ocean. Some people think investing in stocks isn't the same as running a stock market, so understanding the market doesn't matter much—or even at all. This chapter calls that an ignorant take, stressing that before you invest in stocks, you have to know you're surviving in a market. How can you survive in a market you don't understand? You hide inside individual stocks because you're afraid that "low tide" saying will splash you awake; you won't ask about the rises and falls, because the answer might be something you don't want to hear.

qa.q: 如果你現在要從零認識股市，你第一件事會做什麼？本書說應該先了解什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你開戶就衝去買賣，費用、交割規則從沒翻過一眼。首先需要了解市場的遊戲規則，因為市場和規則都不是自己定的，尤其要弄清「如何纔算是賺錢」的規則；其次瞭解市場參與羣體，除自己外還有什麼人參與投資，做到知己知彼。你嫌規則枯燥，是貪快進場；可連遊戲怎麼玩都不清，輸了都怪不到點上。
keywords: 本書說應該先了解什麼
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 You open an account and rush straight into buying and selling, never once glancing at the fees or settlement rules. First you need to understand the rules of the market game—because neither the market nor the rules are set by you—especially the rule of what actually counts as "making money." Second, get to know the crowd in the market: besides you, who else is in the game? Know yourself and know the other side. You find the rules boring because you're too eager to get in fast—but if you don't even know how the game is played, when you lose you can't even pin it on the right thing.

qa.q: 你虧過「不懂規則」的錢嗎？本書說這種虧法屬於什麼性質？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你又虧了一筆，第一反應是罵市場太邪門。因為市場與遊戲規則都不是自己定的，不瞭解就無法在市場裡生存。深入瞭解交易規則、特別是賺錢的規則，才能避免因缺少常識而虧錢，這是認識市場的第一步。不懂規則而虧，是自討苦喫。你賴市場，是死要面子不肯認「是我不懂」；把無知藏起來，下一次照虧。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 You lost another one, and your first move is to curse the market for being too wicked. Because neither the market nor its rules are set by you—if you don't understand them, you can't survive in it. Digging into the trading rules, especially the money-making rules, is the only way to avoid losing money out of sheer ignorance. That's step one of knowing the market. Losing because you don't know the rules is asking for trouble. Blaming the market is just you protecting your pride, refusing to admit "I didn't understand." Hide your ignorance, and next time you'll lose all over again.

qa.q: 你知道跟你對賭的都是些什麼人嗎？本書說瞭解他們有什麼用？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你下單時只算自己帳，從不猜對面那人怎麼想。目的是做到知己知彼：除了自己之外，還要了解還有什麼人參與股票投資，知道自己的對手和同在市場中的參與者，才能在市場裡更好地生存和賺錢。你懶得想對手，是怕一想就發現自己正處下風；逃避這問，虧了才後知後覺。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 When you place an order, you only count your own side, never once guessing what the person across from you is thinking. The point is to know yourself and know the other side: besides you, you need to understand who else is participating in stock investing, who your opponents are, and who else is in the same market—only then can you survive and make money better. You can't be bothered to think about the other side because you're afraid that the moment you do, you'll realize you're on the losing end. Dodge that question and you only wake up after the loss.

qa.q: 同樣是帳戶沒賺錢，一種是「沒本事」，一種是「缺常識」——你屬於哪一種？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你虧了錢，含糊歸咎「運氣差」，不肯細分原因。投資股票不賺錢那是能耐的問題，屬於能力或本事不足；不懂遊戲規則而虧錢，那純粹是缺少常識、自討苦喫。兩者性質不同，後者完全可以靠學習規則避免。你含糊帶過，是怕老實歸類會照出自己的空；承認缺哪一塊，比賴運氣難。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 You lose money and vaguely blame it on "bad luck," refusing to break down the real reasons. Not making money investing in stocks is a skill issue—short on ability or know-how. Losing money because you don't understand the rules is pure lack of common sense, asking for trouble. Those two are totally different, and the latter can absolutely be avoided by just learning the rules. You gloss over it because you're scared that honestly categorizing it will shine a light on your own empty spot—admitting which piece you're missing is harder than blaming luck.

qa.q: 你的精力是花在「瞭解市場」還是「研究個股」上？這個分配比例說明瞭什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你一天盯盤八小時，七大半耗在自己那幾隻上。傳達「市場優先於個股」的理念：投資者生存的環境是整個市場，把精力的重心放在瞭解市場上，而不是隻盯住個別股票，是安全賺錢、避免自討苦喫的前提。你捨不得把時間給大盤，是貪那點盯倉的踏實；可重心歪了，安全賺錢就無從談起。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 You stare at the screen eight hours a day, and seven of those hours go to your own little pile of stocks. This is about getting across the idea that "the market comes before individual stocks": the world an investor survives in is the whole market. Putting your energy into understanding the market, not just fixating on a few individual stocks, is the prerequisite for making money safely and not asking for trouble. You can't bear to give the big picture your time because you're hooked on that little sense of security from staring at your own positions. But once your center of gravity is off, safely making money is out of the question.

qa.q: 你願不願意把「認識市場」當成投資的第一課？本書為什麼把這句話放在開頭？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你一上來就找「必漲指標」，恨不得明天就用。意在強調本章承先啟後的地位：先確立「瞭解市場」的正確理念，後文將系統地幫助投資者認識股票市場，把了解市場當作投資的第一課，值得認真學習。你追指標，是貪那條捷徑；不肯先補「認識市場」這課，地基沒打就急著蓋樓。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 You show up and immediately hunt for a "sure-win indicator," wishing you could use it tomorrow. This is meant to highlight this chapter's role as a bridge: first establish the right mindset of "understanding the market," and later chapters will systematically help investors get to know the stock market. Treat understanding the market as lesson one in investing—it's worth studying seriously. You chase indicators because you're greedy for that shortcut; you won't sit down and catch up on the "know your market" lesson first. The foundation hasn't even been dug, and you're already rushing to build the house.

qa.q: 全職炒股和業餘炒股，哪個更容易成功？你以為的答案和作者的答案一樣嗎？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你也想過辭職在家炒股。但對小資金投資者而言，業餘投資更容易成功；只有資金大到能坐莊、操縱股票價格的人，職業投資才更容易成功。你羨慕的不是他的成績，是那份「不用上班」的自在——羨慕裡藏的是逃避。
qa.a_en: Hey~ 😊 You've thought about quitting your job to day-trade at home too. But for small-capital investors, investing on the side is actually the easier path to success. Only when your money is big enough to act as the market maker and manipulate stock prices does full-time investing become the better bet. What you envy isn't his results—it's that "no need to clock in" freedom. And tucked inside that envy is a little bit of running away.

qa.q: 職業投資者天天盯盤，為什麼反而更容易出錯？錯在哪個環節？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你從九點半坐到三點，一分沒落下。職業者開盤時間守在電腦旁盯盤，股價變動百分百影響其情緒，情緒受擾判斷即失準，所以關注的越多，出錯的概率就越大。你以為自己在收集信息，其實那一整天收集的，全是慌。
keywords: 為什麼反而更容易出錯
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 You sat from 9:30 to 3:00, not missing a single minute. For professionals, once the market opens, they're glued to the screen—price changes 100% affect their emotions, and when emotions get disturbed, judgment goes off. So the more you watch, the higher your chance of messing up. You think you're gathering information, but really, all you gathered that whole day was anxiety.

qa.q: 「常在河邊走，怎能不濕鞋」——作者用這句話說的是誰？濕的是什麼鞋？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你每天在河邊走，還覺得自己腳步很穩。「常在河邊走，怎能不濕鞋」，喻指天天看盤如同在河邊行走，終難避免被行情「弄濕鞋」、做出錯誤決策。你不是不會濕，是每一次濕了都告訴自己下次不會——那份自信，是僥倖。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 You walk by the river every day and still think your footing is solid. 'If you always walk by the river, your shoes are bound to get wet'—it means watching the market daily is like walking along the river, and eventually you can't avoid getting your shoes splashed by the market movements and making wrong decisions. It's not that you never get wet—it's that every time you do, you tell yourself next time will be different. That confidence? That's just luck.

qa.q: 為什麼沒時間看盤的業餘投資者，決策反而更理智？差別在哪裡？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你有沒有發現，出門那天做的決定反而最清醒？開盤時不在電腦旁邊、看不到行情，行情變化對情緒影響不大；情緒不受影響的時候做出的決策基本上都是理智的。所以要你離開盤面，你捨不得——捨不得的不是信息，是怕不在場就錯過了。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 Have you noticed that the decisions you make on days you're out are actually the clearest? When the market opens and you're not at the computer, you can't see the quotes, so market changes don't affect your emotions much. Decisions made when emotions aren't stirred are basically rational. So when we tell you to step away from the screen, you can't bear it—what you can't bear isn't the information, it's the fear that if you're not there, you'll miss something.

qa.q: 一家賣證券軟體的公司，卻從不開發動態行情軟體——你覺得它傻還是聰明？為什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 一家做證券軟體的大公司，幾十年不做即時行情——你想過為什麼嗎？它專向美國股民提供專業證券投資軟體、規模很大，卻從創辦至今從來不開發動態行情軟體，只開發靜態的盤後分析系統。它不給你，是因為知道你一拿到就忍不住；不給，纔是替你著想。
keywords: 一家賣證券軟體的公司
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 A big securities software company—for decades, they never did real-time quotes. Ever wondered why? They provide professional investment software to US stock investors on a huge scale, yet from day one they never developed dynamic quote software—only static post-market analysis systems. They didn't give it to you because they know once you get it, you can't resist. Not giving it to you is actually looking out for you.

qa.q: 作者敬佩那位軟體公司老闆的什麼？他懂的是股票，還是人？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 那個老闆最懂的一件事：股民要的和股民需要的，是兩回事。他不迎合投資人看盤的需求，而是迎合投資股票賺錢的需求，這樣做表明他確實懂股票，更懂得投資股票的人。你每天開的那個視窗，從來只滿足「想看」——想看的那隻手，是手癢。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 The one thing that boss knows best: what stock investors want and what they need are two different things. He doesn't cater to investors' urge to watch the market—he caters to the need to make money from stocks. Doing that shows he truly understands stocks, and even better, understands the people who invest in them. That window you open every day only satisfies the 'want to watch'—and that wanting hand? It's just itchy.

qa.q: 軟體公司「不賣動態行情」這件事，告訴小投資人什麼道理？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 要你一週不看盤，你第一反應是「那怎麼行」。但真正能在股市上賺錢的小投資人應該遠離市場，只有這樣思維纔不會受環境的幹擾，印證了業餘投資更容易賺錢的見解。你那句「怎麼行」，說的是慌——不是怕錯過行情，是怕沒事做。
keywords: 告訴小投資人什麼道理
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 If I told you not to look at the market for a week, your first reaction is 'no way.' But small investors who actually make money in the stock market should stay away from it—only then can their thinking stay free from environmental interference, which backs up the idea that amateur investing is easier to profit from. That 'no way' of yours? That's fear talking—not fear of missing market moves, but fear of having nothing to do.

qa.q: 你盯盤能盯出一個漲停嗎？作者說你的目光對股價和對你自己，分別有什麼作用？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你盯著它看一整天，它一根頭髮都不會動。專心致志地看盤絕對不會影響任何一隻股票價格的走勢，但股價的變動100%能夠影響你的情緒，這是盯盤最大的危害。這場買賣你穩虧：你給的是一整天，換回的是滿滿的情緒——多半是怕。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 You stare at it all day, and it won't move a single hair. Staring intently at the market will never affect the price movement of any stock, but price changes absolutely 100% affect your emotions—that's the biggest danger of watching the screen. This trade you're guaranteed to lose: you give a whole day, and in return you get a load of emotions—mostly fear.

qa.q: 「業餘比職業容易成功」這個結論，對誰成立？對誰不成立？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 這句話你別急著對號入座。這個問題主要針對小資金而言；若能做莊操縱股票價格，職業投資當然更容易成功，故結論僅適用於小投資者。你之所以愛聽，是因為它給了你一個不必檢討自己操作的安慰。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 Don't jump to conclusions about this one. This point mainly applies to small capital; if you can manipulate stock prices as a market maker, professional investing would obviously be more successful, so the conclusion only holds for small investors. The reason you like hearing it? Because it gives you comfort—an excuse not to examine your own trading.

qa.q: 對小資金投資人，作者最終的建議是什麼？你打算照做嗎？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 一週不看盤，你敢嗎？小投資人做業餘投資者更容易賺錢，應該遠離市場，讓思維免受環境幹擾，這正是本章提倡的「化繁為簡、安全賺錢」理念。你不敢試，不是怕錯過，是怕那一週裡沒人告訴你該怎麼辦——那份慌，纔是盤面真正給你的東西。
keywords: 作者最終的建議是什麼
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 Could you go a whole week without checking the market? Small investors actually make money easier as part-time investors by staying away from the market and keeping their minds free from outside noise—that's exactly what this chapter is about: “simplify, stay safe, and make money.” You don't dare try it, not because you're afraid of missing out, but because you're scared that during that week, no one will tell you what to do—that panic, that's what the market really gives you.

qa.q: 手上已經有一套能賺錢的方法，你還會去找第二套嗎？作者說這不是方法問題，是什麼問題？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你收藏夾裡三十七種戰法，用熟的一種都沒有。書裡主張只要擁有一種能賺錢的方法，就不要再去尋找第二種方法，因為這是心態的問題，不是方法的問題。你一直找，不是因為方法不夠好，是貪——總覺得還有更好的在後面。
keywords: 作者說這不是方法問題
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 You've got thirty-seven different strategies saved in your bookmarks, but you haven't actually mastered a single one. The book says if you already have one method that makes money, don't go looking for a second one—because this is a mindset problem, not a method problem. You keep searching, not because the methods aren't good enough, but because of greed—you always feel like something better is waiting out there.

qa.q: 已經能賺錢還到處找新方法的人，心裡在盼什麼？這個盼頭錯在哪裡？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你說「我想做得更好」，聽起來很上進。這類人大多抱有希望賺得更多、做得更好的期望，這種心態容易讓人忘記投資股票的目的是賺錢，而不是尋找方法。你那個「更好」，量的不是收益，是面子——方法越冷門，講起來越漂亮。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 You say “I want to do better,” and that sounds really ambitious. But people like this often hold the expectation of making more and performing better, and that mindset makes you forget that the goal of investing in stocks is to make money, not to hunt for methods. That “better” you're chasing isn't measured in returns—it's measured in face. The more obscure the method, the fancier it sounds when you talk about it.

qa.q: 一直找新方法的人，最後的錢去了哪裡？作者用哪句話點破結局？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你買過幾套教程、幾個指標？加起來也是一筆錢。最終你的錢會全部用來檢驗所獲得方法的準確性，錢財耗盡卻未必換來更準的方法，完全偏離了投資賺錢的目的。你花得很爽，是因為花錢那一刻，買到的是「我快要學成了」的安慰。
keywords: 作者用哪句話點破結局
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 How many tutorial courses and indicators have you bought? Add them all up—that's real money. In the end, all your money will be spent testing the accuracy of the methods you've obtained, and you might burn through it without ever finding a more precise approach, totally losing sight of why you invest in the first place: to make money. You enjoy spending because in that moment, what you're really buying is the comfort of thinking, “I'm almost there.”

qa.q: 換了一百種方法，最後的動作是什麼？作者說投資的本質有多枯燥？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你以為高手每天都很精彩。書裡認為股票投資實際上就是一種簡單的、行為反覆的重複，枯燥而乏味；不管哪種方法，其最後的結果都是買進、賣出。你受不了這種枯燥，是手癢——一枯燥就覺得自己沒在努力。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 You think pros have exciting days every day. But the book says stock investing is actually a simple, repetitive behavior—dull and boring. No matter what method you use, the end result is always buying and selling. You can't stand that boredom because your hands get itchy—the moment things feel dull, you think you're not working hard enough.

qa.q: 為什麼再新的花樣也改變不了投資的無聊？作者的理由是什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你換方法，多半不是因為它失效了。因為無論哪種方法，其最後的結果都是買進、賣出，方法再多也改變不了投資行為簡單重複的本質，所以不必求新求變。你換的是新鮮感，躲的是重複一百次的枯燥；說穿了，是忍不住。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 The reason you switch methods usually isn't because the old one stopped working. Because no matter which method you choose, the final result is still buying and selling—more methods can't change the fact that investing is essentially simple repetition. So there's no need to chase novelty. What you're really chasing is a fresh feeling, and what you're avoiding is the boredom of doing the same thing a hundred times. Bottom line? You just can't help yourself.

qa.q: 換方法換不停，表面看是方法問題，作者說實質是什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你換過七次方法，每一次都說「這次不一樣」。尋找更多方法看似是方法問題，實質是心態問題；問題不在方法本身好壞，而在於貪多求新、不安於使用既有方法的心態。你不是不信那個方法，是不甘心一輩子只用一招——那太不厲害了。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 You've switched methods seven times now, and every time you say “this time it's different.” Hunting for more methods looks like a method problem, but it's really a mindset issue. The problem isn't whether the methods are good or bad—it's your mindset of wanting more, craving novelty, and being unable to settle for what you already have. It's not that you don't trust the method. It's that you're not willing to use just one trick for the rest of your life—that just doesn't feel impressive enough.

qa.q: 你來股市是為了「錢」還是為了「方法」？這個答案怎麼指導你選方法？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 問你來市場幹什麼，你答「賺錢」；看你每天在做什麼，是研究戰法。來市場的目的是為了錢而不是方法，所以只要方法能賺錢就足夠了，沒有必要再去尋找第二種方法。研究比操作有趣，因為研究錯了不用承認虧錢。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 If I ask why you came to the market, you'd say “to make money.” But look at what you do every day—you're studying strategies. You came for money, not methods, so as long as a method makes money, that's enough. There's no need to go looking for a second one. Researching is more fun than trading because when you're researching, you don't have to admit you lost money when you're wrong.

qa.q: 作者給你的操作建議，具體到「錢」和「方法」怎麼分配？你聽得進去嗎？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 一套方法用滿一百次，你敢不敢？擁有一種能賺錢的方法之後就不要再尋找第二種方法，安心反覆使用既有方法，把金錢用於賺錢本身，而非用來檢驗新方法的準確性。你不敢，是因為用到第二十次還沒見效，就得承認是自己不行——怪方法容易多了。
qa.a_en: Heyyy~ 😊 Would you dare to use one single method a full hundred times? Once you've found a way to make money, stop looking for a second one. Settle down and keep using what already works — spend your money on making money itself, not on testing whether some new approach actually works. You don't dare, because if you try it twenty times and still don't see results, you'd have to admit it's on you — blaming the method is way easier.

qa.q: 「想賺更多、想做得更好」聽起來很上進，作者為什麼說它不好？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 「想做得更好」這句話，最難看出它是壞的。這種期望會讓人忘記投資股票的目的是賺錢，轉而為尋找方法而尋找方法，最終本末倒置，把全部資金浪費在檢驗方法的準確性上。它難識破，是因為披著上進的外衣——你越勤奮，越不忍心承認自己在繞路。
qa.a_en: Heyyy~ 😊 "I just want to do better" — that's the hardest thing to recognize as bad. That kind of expectation makes you forget that the whole point of investing in stocks is to make money, and instead you end up searching for methods just for the sake of searching. In the end you've got it backwards — wasting all your capital on testing whether your methods are accurate. It's hard to see through because it wears the disguise of self-improvement — the harder you work, the less willing you are to admit you've been going in circles.

qa.q: 你覺得自己賺得少，是因為「本金太小」嗎？作者說這其實是什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 「要是本金多點，我早賺了」——這句話你對自己說過幾年了？書裡說得很白：本金大小不是影響你盈利多少的主要因素，把本金小當成制約利益的瓶頸只是一種藉口或假象，真正決定盈虧的是投資人的能耐。藉口好找，能耐難練，所以你寧可天天怪本金，也不肯承認該練的是自己。
qa.a_en: Heyyy~ 😊 "If only I had more capital, I'd already be rich" — how many years have you been telling yourself that? The book says it plainly: the size of your capital isn't the main factor in how much profit you make. Treating small capital as the bottleneck holding back your gains is just an excuse or an illusion. What really determines your profit or loss is your skill as an investor. Excuses are easy to find, but skill is hard to build — so you'd rather blame your capital every day than admit it's yourself that needs the work.

qa.q: 一萬塊變成億萬富翁，你覺得是神話嗎？作者說它缺的只是什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你覺得一萬塊起步是笑話，所以從沒認真算過——可書裡偏偏算給你看：因為股市對有能耐的人是天堂，擁有較小的本金可以賺到很多錢，一萬塊錢變成億萬富翁絕不是神話故事，小本金照樣能滾成巨額財富。你怕的不是算術，是怕那個能滾的人，真的會是自己。
keywords: 作者說它缺的只是什麼
qa.a_en: Heyyy~ 😊 You think starting with ten thousand is a joke, so you've never seriously done the math — but the book goes ahead and does it for you: because the stock market is heaven for capable people, even a small amount of capital can make a fortune. Turning ten thousand into a billion isn't a fairy tale — small capital can absolutely roll into huge wealth. What you're afraid of isn't the arithmetic. It's that the person who could actually roll it up... might really be you.

qa.q: 沒有本事的人，就算有億萬家財，在股市裡的下場是什麼？要多長時間？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你總說「等我資金大了再說」，好像錢一多就自然會賺。書裡把另一面翻給你：因為沒有賺錢本領的人縱然擁有億萬家財，變成窮光蛋也不會很難，所需要的時間也不會很長，大本金也保不住。你等的那天不會自己來——你不肯承認，問題從來不在錢，在你那套沒變過的本事。
keywords: 在股市裡的下場是什麼
qa.a_en: Heyyy~ 😊 You always say "I'll wait until I have more money," as if having more money automatically means you'll know how to make more. The book shows you the other side: because someone without the skill to make money — even if they own billions — can become broke without much difficulty, and it won't take that long either. Even big capital won't save you. The day you're waiting for won't come on its own — what you won't admit is that the problem was never the money. It's the same old skill set you've never changed.

qa.q: 兩萬塊、每次賺20%、交易48次——作者算出的結果是什麼？你信這個算法嗎？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你第一次聽這道算術題時眼睛發亮，對不對？書裡算得沒錯：假如你有2萬元的本金，每次盈利20%，交易48次之後你理論上已是億萬富翁（理想化計算，未計交易成本與回撤），因此無須擔憂自己的本金太小。問題從來不在算法，在「每次20%」那一格——你不敢往下填，是怕答案讓自己難堪。
qa.a_en: Heyyy~ 😊 Your eyes lit up the first time you heard this math problem, didn't they? The book's calculation is right: if you start with 20,000 in capital and make 20% profit each time, after 48 trades you're already a billionaire — so there's no need to worry about your capital being too small. The problem was never the math. It's that little box that says "20% each time" — you don't dare fill it in, because you're afraid the answer will embarrass you.

qa.q: 與其抱怨本金小，你該把力氣花在哪裡？作者給的方向是什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 「等我有錢了再好好學」——這句藉口你用了多少年？書裡要你倒過來做：應拋棄把本金小當作瓶頸的觀念，轉而專注提升自己的操作本領，靠正確的方法讓小本金透過一路滾上去持續滾動壯大。你把「學」排在「有錢」後面，它就永遠輪不到。
qa.a_en: Heyyy~ 😊 "Once I'm rich, then I'll really learn" — how many years have you been using that excuse? The book tells you to flip it around: throw away the idea that small capital is your bottleneck, and instead focus on leveling up your trading skills. Use the right method and let your small capital keep rolling forward, growing and compounding along the way. If you put "learning" after "being rich," it'll never be your turn.

qa.q: 最該關注的不是本金，那是什麼？作者反覆強調的兩個字是什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你一遍遍算「要是本金多十倍就好了」，卻很少算自己這一年本事長了多少。書裡的答案兩個字：能耐——投資人最應該關注的不是本金，而是自己的能耐；本金大小不是影響收益的主要因素，本領高低纔是關鍵。盯著帳戶裡的數字，你只會愈看愈不甘；盯著自己上一次犯的錯，纔是真在長本事。
qa.a_en: Heyyy~ 😊 You keep calculating "if only my capital were ten times bigger," but you rarely calculate how much your skill has grown this year. The book's answer is just two words: capability. What an investor should focus on most isn't their capital — it's their own capability. The size of your capital isn't the main factor in your returns; how skilled you are is what actually matters. Staring at the numbers in your account, all you'll feel is more and more resentment. But staring at the last mistake you made? That's how you actually grow.

qa.q: 「本金小不是藉口」落到操作上，你該怎麼做？第一步是什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你拿「就這點錢，學了也白學」當藉口，連書都懶得翻開。書裡給的恰恰相反：不要因本金小而放棄或畏縮，集中精力學習正確的理念與方法，追求每次穩定盈利，讓小資金在多次交易中累積成鉅富。你嫌錢少不肯練，錢也嫌你沒本事，不肯來。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 You're using "with this little money, learning is pointless" as an excuse and can't even be bothered to open a book. The book says the exact opposite: don't give up or shrink back just because your capital is small. Focus on learning the right principles and methods, aim for steady profits every time, and let small capital grow into huge wealth through many trades. You complain your money is too little to practice, but money also complains you're not skilled enough to come to you.

qa.q: 本章和「安全賺錢」有什麼關係？為什麼「能耐」纔是根本？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你每天刷新帳戶餘額的次數比翻書還多——可數字不會自己變大。本書在這裡提醒你：提醒投資人把注意力從資金量轉向賺錢能力，只有具備能耐才能安全地長期獲利，能力纔是財富增長的真正根本。你不敢把目光從餘額挪開，是怕承認自己能耐不夠——那太沒面子。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 You refresh your account balance more times a day than you open a book—but the numbers won't grow by themselves. This book is here to remind you: shift your focus from the size of your capital to your ability to make money. Only when you have real skill can you profit safely over the long term. Ability is the true foundation of wealth growth. You're afraid to take your eyes off the balance because you don't want to admit your skill isn't good enough—that would be too embarrassing.

qa.q: 為什麼「本金太小」不是原因，而是藉口？真正被藏起來的是什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 「要是我有五萬本金，早翻倍了」——你一虧就說這句話，可它替你擋掉的是真相。因為把賺得少歸咎於本金太小，迴避了真正的原因——自身能力不足；本金大小並非影響收益的主要因素，故屬藉口與假象。你罵了本金一年，它替你背了本該你背的鍋。
keywords: 真正被藏起來的是什麼
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 "If I had fifty grand in capital, I'd have doubled it already"—you say this every time you lose, but what it's really shielding you from is the truth. Because blaming your small capital for earning too little lets you avoid the real reason—your own lack of ability. The size of your capital isn't the main factor affecting returns, so it's just an excuse and an illusion. You've been cursing your capital for a year, and it's been carrying the blame that should've been yours all along.

qa.q: 作者對本金小的你，想傳達什麼信心？這份信心建立在什麼之上？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你缺的不是那筆「夠大的本金」，是肯相信小錢也能練出本事的開始。書裡給的信心很實在：小本金同樣具備致富的可能，關鍵在於有沒有能耐；只要方法正確並持續獲利，小資金也能成就大財富，無須擔憂本金太小。怕的是你連第一步都嫌小，不敢邁出去。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 What you're missing isn't that "big enough pile of capital"—it's the willingness to believe that even small money can build real skill. The book gives you solid confidence: small capital can absolutely lead to wealth—the key is whether you have the ability. As long as your method is right and you keep profiting, small capital can create big wealth, no need to worry about it being too small. The real fear is you thinking even the first step is too small to take.

qa.q: 你心裡有沒有崇拜的「股神」？作者為什麼說崇拜他幫不了你？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你手機裡存著股神語錄，虧了就拿出來讀一遍，彷彿讀了能沾上他的運氣。書裡說得很冷：主張股市是孤獨的行業，一個人在戰鬥，每個人要戰勝的對手是自己而不是別人。對方之所以成功，是因為他戰勝了自己，崇拜他並不能幫你戰勝自己。你崇拜的是他，怕面對的是自己。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 You've got stock-guru quotes saved on your phone, and every time you lose money you read one again, as if reading it would rub off some of his luck. The book puts it coldly: it says the stock market is a lonely business, you're fighting alone, and the opponent everyone has to beat is yourself, not someone else. That person succeeded because he beat himself—worshipping him won't help you beat yourself. You admire him but are afraid to face yourself.

qa.q: 你現在最大的問題，是「看不懂行情」還是「看不懂自己」？作者說是哪個？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你研究巴菲特比研究自己還用心——他的每一筆買賣你倒背如流，自己為什麼虧卻說不清。作者認為現在面臨的問題是如何戰勝你自己，因此瞭解你自己就顯得非常重要，而不是去崇拜他人。你寧可研究別人，也不肯承認：最該研究的那個人，一直坐在螢幕這頭。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 You study Buffett more carefully than you study yourself—you know every trade he's ever made by heart, but you can't even explain why you lose. The author believes the real challenge now is how to beat yourself, so understanding yourself is extremely important—not worshipping others. You'd rather study someone else than admit this: the person you should be studying most has been sitting right on this side of the screen.

qa.q: 崇拜一個你根本不瞭解的人，最壞的結果是什麼？作者說會「丟」了什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你學大神的姿勢越來越像，有一天會發現鏡子裡的人已經不是自己——書裡警告的就是這個：不瞭解對方的盲目崇拜只會把你自己也搞丟了，這可能是股票投資之外的一種損失，即連自我都迷失了。你模仿得越用力，離自己越遠——等鏡子裡那人你都不認得了，再慌就晚了。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 The more you mimic a master's moves, the more one day you'll look in the mirror and realize the person there is no longer you—the book warns exactly about this: blindly worshipping someone you don't understand will only make you lose yourself too. This could be a loss beyond stock investing—losing your own identity. The harder you try to imitate, the further you drift from yourself—by the time you don't even recognize the person in the mirror, it'll be too late to panic.

qa.q: 巴菲特拿得住、你也拿得住嗎？他的成功憑什麼不能複製到你身上？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你照著大神的單子買，賺了覺得是自己聰明，虧了怪自己沒學到位——可你從一開始就錯了。因為你不是他們，他的成功並不能代表你能成功；同樣，失敗者不能成功也不代表你不會成功，因為你不是他，成敗無法移植。你羨慕他，卻怕承認：自己扛不住他那條路。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 You copy the master's trades, and when you win you think it's because you're smart, when you lose you blame yourself for not learning well enough—but you were wrong from the start. Because you're not them. Their success doesn't mean you'll succeed; likewise, a loser failing doesn't mean you'll fail either, because you're not them. Success and failure can't be transplanted. You envy him, but you're afraid to admit: you couldn't handle the path he walks.

qa.q: 你嘴裡談著巴菲特，但你瞭解他承受過什麼嗎？作者想讓你看見什麼？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你羨慕巴菲特拿得住，卻沒想過他拿的那幾年夜裡是怎麼過的。書裡點醒你：巴菲特一隻股票能拿好幾年，這好幾年當中的壓力未必是你能體會與承受的；談論巴菲特卻不瞭解巴菲特，正說明不要崇拜、要審視自身。你扛不住的那幾年下跌，正是你不肯承認的差距。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 You envy Buffett for holding stocks long-term, but you've never thought about what those years felt like for him at night. The book hits you with a truth: Buffett can hold a stock for years—but the pressure during those years may not be something you can even imagine or bear. Talking about Buffett without really understanding him just shows you shouldn't worship him—you should examine yourself instead. Those years of decline you can't stomach are exactly the gap you refuse to admit.

qa.q: 作者最後讓你做什麼？「做自己」三個字，在股市裡具體是什麼意思？
qa.a: 哈嘍～😊 你上一次「完全照自己的想法」下單是什麼時候？恐怕要想很久。書裡的答案簡單到你不肯信：不要崇拜任何人，好好地做你自己。成功的關鍵在於瞭解並戰勝自己，而不是把希望寄託在效仿偶像之上。你不敢做自己，是怕虧了之後，連怪別人的藉口都沒了。
qa.a_en: Hey there~ 😊 When was the last time you placed an order 'purely following your own idea'? Probably takes a while to remember. The answer in the book is so simple you'd refuse to believe it: don't worship anyone, just be yourself. The key to success lies in understanding and overcoming yourself, not pinning your hopes on imitating idols.
